Date: April 27, 1955 From: Secretary O. Dvortsova To: #bulletin_board_archive  Goran Višnjić's edited article for the bulletin board:  "As chemists, we know better than anyone how addictions and dangerous drugs are fatal for any society. And today we'll talk about opium—not the illicit drug, but the kind "of the masses"—religion. My colleagues, you know that a new religious movement has appeared in the world, namely the so-called Church of the Kollektiv. I can already see your grins and hear your venomous jokes, but the situation is extremely dangerous! The Kollektiv was created as a triumph of mankind and science, but any religion is the antithesis of these things! Religion compels people to have faith, not knowledge; to obey rather than create! How weak must humans still be if they search for hope in their own fantasies even in this age when reason has prevailed..."

Date: March 29, 1955 From: Head of the Ecosystems Department I. Baver To: Junior Lab Tech E. Basinskaya  Ekaterina, I deny your request to drain the swamps using robots. Understand that our swamps are a unique biome, unparalleled on the entire planet! The potential for research, including terraforming experiments, is inconceivable! They aren't a puddle you can dig out with a shovel. They're a real wonder of nature! P.S. Get some rubber boots from the supply manager and don't intrude on nature.

Date: June 3, 1955 From: Facility 3826 Deputy Director M. Stockhausen To: #mendeleev #management  Order from Comrade Sechenov, Director of Facility 3826  All employees of Facility 3826, including service employees, are to undergo polymerization on June 10th, 1955. Make sure everyone signs the protocol after the procedure.

Date: February 3, 1954 From: Robo-Theater Director S. Lastochkin To: Senior Lab Assistant K. Vorobyaninov  My dear fellow, I must say, I am extremely disappointed by your refusal! It seems you lack any understanding of the prospects and practical applications of my idea! You hole up completely in your labs, claiming you don't have time! You churn out so many different chemicals day in and day out, so you should make one for us... a compound for... uh, a romantic atmosphere! You have plenty of time, but no imagination! If you would deign to attend even one meeting of our special club at the Theater, I'm sure you would change your mind! You don't drink, you don't smoke, you don't chase girls... My friend, you're just sick! With organizational impotence and pallid infirmity! Extremely disappointed! Extremely! At least think about it!

Date: June 4, 1955 From: Research Assistant K. Fomin To: Research Assistant A. Arbatova  Hey, I found out yesterday that the acid-base indicator we've been using, phenolphthalein, has laxative properties. But it's also bitter. I want to prank Zhenya Burak—I'll have to mask the taste so I can add it to a beer!

Date: June 4, 1955 From: Senior Lab Assistant V. Vinnik To: Research Assistant A. Shvedovchenko  Yesterday, my graduate student mentioned that they and their comrades procured bromoacetone tear gas. I do not know if they managed to synthesize it, but I would recommend wearing a gas mask to enter that lab unless you want to shed crocodile tears. They spilled it or something. What a mess!

Date: March 4, 1954 From: Senior Programmer of the Logic Department E. Amperyan To: Secretary O. Dvortsova  Oksana Viktorovna, when I called you a biorobot I didn't mean to offend you! Just the opposite! Look, from a scientific—and even medical—point of view, there is no difference between humans and robots. Both move limbs (if they aren't broken) according to identical principles: an electrical impulse travels from a source to a point and starts chemical reactions. When I said you're "like a biorobot" I was admiring your health recovery after the fracture, not mocking you! I ask you again to forgive me—for these words and for an invitation to go skiing at the beginning of spring!

Date: March 4, 1955 From: Junior Lab Tech E. Basinskaya To: #bulletin_board_archive  In the city of Rybinsk in the Yaroslavl Region, some young Octobrists who toured the Facility have created their own "complex." In scare quotes, of course—this is more of a game than something serious. They call it the NITWITT Complex, which derives from the "National Institute for the Technology of Witchcraft and Thaumaturgy." They play such sweet games there—magic wands driven by quantum entanglements, invisibility cloaks supposedly based on the refraction of light, GOST-compliant spells, and that sort of thing. I think we should do a story, highlighting that modern science is real magic, and send them some educational gift.

Date: April 5, 1955 From: Security Department Officer I. Vitvinin To: Senior Scientific Group Director Zh. Shatalina  Dear Zhanna Arkadyevna,  Your inquiry has been reviewed. A strange goose implanted with a THOUGHT device has indeed been running around the Mendeleev Complex. Based on security camera data, he seems to have been thrown over the fence on the night of April 1 by several people wearing the uniform of the Pavlov Complex. Unfortunately, we were not able to make out the identities of these employees. We have also not managed to capture the goose. I can't say for sure, as I have no expertise in these matters, but it must be some kind of experimental specimen because it is much faster and more aggressive than an ordinary village bird. Not to mention that it swears like a sailor. We have made several attempts to catch it, involving robotic personnel, but to no avail. Unfortunately, we cannot continue to waste our security resources chasing a wild goose, even such a talkative one. As long as it does not pose a serious threat to the operation of the complex and its employees' work, we will continue to monitor and come up with a future solution. P.S. Its voice sounds familiar, somehow...

Date: June 15, 1955 From: Secretary O. Dvortsova To: Physics and Chemistry Professor A. Kheimsov  Listen, professor, I don't share your joy. Yes, people are returning to work, and that's great. The hotel is already overflowing with patients sent for treatment as well as guests, however... the Mendeleev itself is still empty. Did you notice? And that's very depressing. Do you know what else, professor? I have a strong foreboding. Everyone thinks the breach is behind us and ahead lies only a future that, though clouded by tragedy, is bright. But for some reason I think this story isn't over yet. I know you loathe my pessimism, but my intuition has never failed me. Be vigilant.

Date: May 7, 1954 From: Senior Officer of the Academy of Consequences Control Department V. Aksakov To: #control_department #academy_of_consequences  Who was responsible for filling out the card for Poly? It's an utter disgrace! No precise description of the action. No causal analysis! What does "changes color according to mood" mean?! What's a mood—have we even defined it? How does a polymer blob in the pigment understand this "mood"? How does it act on the carrier? On top of all that, don't you think its use would be limited for an entire class of employees, like Argentum and others who work "in the field." Comrade Filatova has already asked and is interested. I remind you, she's one of the top brass! And bosses with green hair—this is just atrocious!

A hard-working specialist from the younger generation of doctors, Eduard Furman does everything in his power to try to attain his mentor Dr. Domov's level of skill. Patients and colleagues have often noticed Furman subconsciously copying not only his superior's work style, but also his ordinary mannerisms, gestures, and even speech. Comrade Furman does not yet fully realize that he has already earned a place at the hospital by dint of his hard work and has no need to imitate Comrade Domov.

Dr. Lizova is an outstanding specialist in the field of endocrinology. She could have become an excellent practitioner, but she preferred management to medicine and is now the Pavlov Complex Hospital's head physician. Thanks to her leadership skills, she has managed to not only assemble a team of top-notch specialists, but also attract the attention of Comrade Pavlov himself. The hospital is now one of the most high-tech stationary medical facilities overseen personally by Pavlov.

A celebrated engineer and machine builder, Makhnyov did not leave Facility 3826 when he retired, but continued working there, becoming the well-known and well-liked cable car station master at Vavilov Complex. His pleasant, amiable demeanor always puts smiles on the faces of employees as they hurry to work.  "Without Ludwig, this place would grind to a halt!" is a common phrase among passengers.

An engineer, roboticist, and programmer, Petrov began his career at the roboticized Maya Plisetskaya Theater as it was in the midst of its most transformative upgrades. He has shown himself to be a talented and inventive specialist with a certain amount of creative vision. Comrade Petrov has an excellent grasp of art, which has helped him make friends with the director of the roboticized theater, as well as Facility 3826 Deputy Director Michael Stockhausen, a well-known aesthete and patron of the arts. Thanks to his friendship with Comrade Stockhausen, Petrov was able to demonstrate his skills and the fruits of his academic labor to Comrade Sechenov himself. The head of the Facility greatly appreciated the young programmer's hard work and pragmatism, which led to Petrov being assigned to a leading position in his scientific team dedicated to the development of the Kollektiv 2.0 neural network.  He has since been found guilty of treason and sentenced to community service at Vavilov Complex.  #.KEY: //Msg. start// Screw you and your military swagger, Major! You'll never take me alive! I'm a superior being. You're just a jackal!//Msg. end//#REG.ENTRY: #June111955

Unfortunately, not all new employees are able to successfully integrate with the Facility 3826 team—especially if their position fails to meet their own expectations. The keeper of the legendary Aniva, a Japanese lighthouse from the distant eastern island of Sakhalin, Khozin has found himself unable to adapt to modern reality. Nostalgia for his old life, robot patrols, and the occasional tour groups from Almaty, Kazakhstan that pass his lighthouse have rendered this lonely, unsociable man even more introverted.

Like the entire interactive entertainment and middleware development department, this high-profile specialist of Polish and Greek descent has made every effort to help the Facility achieve its goals. Overcoming all the challenges of his intense and important work easily and with a smile, Comrade Altupolis proudly delivered a truly fascinating video game that has since become part of Kollektiv 2.0's software. As a result, he received accolades from his coworkers, took a vacation to Gagra, Georgia, and received a financial incentive from the Facility. Huzzah, Comrades! Glory to the heroes of Soviet labor, and long live video games!
What kind of robots would the United States have?

Comrade Grabov's career began in 1941, when he was forced to drive a train carrying coal to the front lines while under Fascist fire despite having no experience. His uncle had taken him inside the engineer's cabin, but was heavily wounded by shrapnel from an exploding shell. Instead of panicking, the young nephew took the controls and managed to drive the train to the troops' position. This feat earned him a medal for bravery and set the young man on his life's path, which would always be bound up with trains. Grabov is fond of saying that "a train needs to ride the track to the end, to the last inch, and get the job done."

A typical engineering manager, Veritayev is strict, rude, loud, and demanding, but still quite competent and knowledgeable. The VDNH's technical staff is all under his direction, and his team has won several awards for superior performance despite the odd magnet-related mishap.

Kollektiv 2.0 is launched! This is a grand day in human history! To all my colleagues and all the progressive minds on the planet, congratulations on the dawn of this historic new age of the evolved mind! That said, the Mendeleev Complex has no connection with the Kollektiv because of the blockade of NORA, whose hostility has grown by an order of magnitude. As a result, manual recombination remains the only way to fix the worsening malfunction in her control circuits. Unfortunately, Agent P-3's sudden disappearance has significantly complicated the recombination process. NORA refuses contact with me and demonstrates murderous aggression against anyone who tries to interact with her via repair vendors. I recommend physically disabling all of NORA's repair vendors until this deadly situation is resolved. I am still preparing the reference algorithms.

Professor A.V. Lebedev's lab notes One hour ago, I received reports that NORA has independently disconnected from the Kollektiv 1.0 network and blocked all incoming communication lines. NORA is not responding to requests. I am urgently flying to the Mendeleev Complex, where I will attempt to solve the problem on site. It is early in the morning, and none of my assistants are in the lab, but there is no time to wait for personnel to arrive.

I managed to repel the attack, but the situation is deplorable: the ORB flight control system has stopped working, and I cannot repair it by myself. After weighing all the pros and cons, and in view of the hostilities staged by our enemies after the Kollektiv 2.0 launch, I have decided to stay here and not be evacuated by the military. I continue my preparations for the manual recombination process.

A junior Vavilov employee, Neyelova was recruited to Facility 3826 as a lab assistant due to her excellent performance in graduate school and various internships. She is interested in genetic modification, has studied botany, and has proven to be very responsible and driven. Her husband is currently serving as a Navy watchman in Kamchatka.

Raguzin is a young Vavilov engineer and an orphan who lost his parents to the Brown Plague during the war. He is an introvert, but also a very talented genetic engineer who has set the record as the youngest specialist at the Facility and the one who has performed the most successful genetic experiments. His most interesting papers, which include "Mobile Plant-Based Cattle Feed" and "Self-Replicating, Fast-Growing Plants," have won him a number of awards.
Zinaida Petrovna Muravyova is a communications officer. She joined a group of the Kollektiv's radical enemies. Use extreme caution. Inform security of her location.

Nikolai Vavilov is a geneticist and botanist. He led botanical expeditions to Western Europe, Asia, Africa, North America, and South America that have enabled him to identify the original sites of the morphogenesis of plants. Vavilov laid the foundation for the study of plant immunity and discovered the law of the homological series in the hereditary variation of organisms. He oversaw the creation of the world's largest collection of cultivated plant seeds, created the system used by the Soviet government to test varieties of cultivated plants, and formulated the principles that now govern the activities of the country's primary agrarian sciences center.  Now in charge of Vavilov Complex, one of the largest complexes of Facility 3826, Vavilov breeds new species of plants in order to expand our planet's agricultural potential and prepare for the ongoing plan to colonize outer space.

An appointee from Leningrad, Smirnov was tasked by the Party with monitoring individual Complex employees. Despite the fact that his role as a "snitch" is well known, he is respected by his coworkers, first and foremost as a host of leisure activities and educational clubs.

A legendary scholar of imperial Russia and later the Soviet Union, Pavlov is the oldest employee of Facility 3826, having reached the truly remarkable age of 106. He met Sechenov soon before his last heart operation, which saved the inventor's life. He is in charge of the complex that bears his name, where he studies the capabilities of biological species, programmable mutations, and progressive medicine.

The BEA-Ds will deliver the carriers with the reference algorithms to the loading room, and the neural puppets will put them in the case of the pneumo-uploader. NORA still won't answer my requests and is blocking all entrances to the complex. To gain access more quickly, I decided to use a local Burav. It dug a shaft that goes from the swamps into the complex. NORA will not be able to block it.

Soviet radio performer Vera Vershinina's incredible, poignant voice became legendary throughout the Soviet Union when she was chosen to become the voice of the Deimos OS virtual assistant in June 1950. Comrade Vershinina's personality and vocal tone was so well-liked at the Chelomey Design Bureau that she quickly become the official voice of Facility 3826. If you talk to a computer, it will answer you in Comrade Vershinina's voice.

Burak was recently appointed to the post of exhibit curator by the Ministry of Culture. Despite his magnificent recommendations and excellent work history, he has struggled to fit in at the strict, buttoned-down VDNH. The HR department receives complaints about his rudeness, excessive familiarity, and condescending attitude toward employees on a nearly weekly basis. However, upper management has been extremely positive about the new hire, noting his fresh perspective on how exhibit pieces are presented and implemented. "Comrade Burak has such an innovative view of things that impetuous new behaviors are always just a step away," said a complaint against Comrade Burak filed on behalf of the VDNH Tour Guide Union.

A German scientist of Jewish descent, Stockhausen worked as a doctor in Berlin during the war. He lived through the first outbreaks of the Brown Plague and was later saved by Soviet soldiers. Prior to his infection, he had an incredible memory—a fact his coworkers could attest to—but lost this ability after the onset of the illness and never demonstrated it again (although he does not regret the loss).  Thanks to his scientific and organizational talents, Stockhausen's career enjoyed a startlingly rapid ascent. He was recruited to the Facility in order to fill a quota for scientists from the German Soviet Socialist Republic and quickly earned Sechenov's respect. Despite his German pedantry and a certain degree of snobbishness, he remains one of the best-known—and best-liked—members of the Facility 3826 team. He is perfectly capable of speaking Russian without an accent, but chooses to "sound German" in order to remind people of his origins.

Sherman was sent to Vavilov in order to fill a quota for specialists from the German Soviet Socialist Republic. Her primary specialization isn't plants or genes, but rather designing essential equipment and reviewing requests from specialists in various fields.

Few people have met the director of the AoC, who is also a leading Soviet programmer and the creator of the Aldan supercomputer. Most employees don't even know that this man exists, but he has actually replaced Comrade Lebedev as the head of the Academy of Consequences' top-secret Neptune facility.

Although his last name is derived from the Russian word for "caramel," Karamelkin is anything but sweet. Everyone knows that he is excessively rude to rule-breakers and can even get physical with more serious violators. Despite this, there is no denying that the theft of drugs and equipment has been reduced fourfold since he assumed his current position. Comrade Karamelkin is fully cognizant of his place at the Facility and in the world at large. Some aspects of his personality suggest a high degree of discipline, while others are nothing more than bad habits. "Everything's fine," Karamelkin mutters before returning to his usual duties.

Comrade Lastochkin is not a traditional theater director. Better known as "Stefan," Lastochkin has had a stunning career, starting out as an office manager and becoming the head of what is perhaps the most famous theater in the world. In less than a year, unique performances such as "The Binding Screws of Friendship," "In the Vice of Passion," and the modern classic "Electric Origins" have become sensations among fans of avant-garde art. However, his narcissism, shady dealings, and despotic management style have set many theater employees at odds with the ambitious new director.

The new neuropolymeric clusters are ready and placed in the module capsules. I decided to use the BEA-Ds I currently have at my disposal to transport the capsules to the loading room. I loaded the BEA-D+ with a launch fragment of the entire recombination, whose neuropolymer carrier is larger and has a higher capacity. Because BEA-Ds are autonomous, I will be able to deliver the capsules to the loading room despite NORA's resistance.

The theater's new office manager, Surkov is an elderly, experienced man who has worked at the Bolshoi and overseen performances on the front lines for soldiers. An honest, but also one-dimensional and somewhat cantankerous old man, Surkov often has harsh words for management and anyone else who draws his ire.

A recent hire, Vishnevskaya was brought on to replace a senior programmer who was fired for inappropriate conduct. She is known as a suffragette, social activist, and active proponent of women's rights. Vishnevskaya is beloved by her coworkers for her responsibility and friendliness.

Elena Krayeva is an exemplary Soviet citizen. Carefree and outgoing, she has long been a regular sight at Pavlov Complex cultural events. Along with her pleasant, friendly personality, Comrade Krayeva is also known for her great passion for her work and has been recognized as a hero of communist labor three years in a row.

One of the leading dog trainers in the Soviet Union, or "Pavlov's Dog," as he jokingly calls himself, Gromyko is a crucial member of the Facility 3826 staff. His published works on raising, training, and cross-breeding species have been translated into 64 languages, five of them by himself. However, despite all his talents and service to the Motherland, this modest dog breeder prefers the company of his four-legged friends to scientific debates. Especially valuable in light of Polymer-based biotechnology is his work on breeding and training martian and lunar "dogs," i.e. the Polymer-based organisms known as Plyusch, which, thanks to Comrade Gromyko's hard work and care, are now exemplary, obedient representatives of man's future interplanetary best friend.

One of the highest-ranking leaders in the Communist Party, Molotov is also the President of the Council of Ministers and a political opponent of Comrade Sechenov. A talented politician used to operate on an international scale, he was made the overseer of Facility 3826 by the CPSU Central Committee and the Council of Ministers.

One of the Facility's managers, Yelizarova is in charge of the VDNH's exhibits and visitor interaction. She stood out from the very beginning of her tenure at the Facility and is responsible for the creation of the VDNH. Rumor has it she had to personally convince Dr. Sechenov of the need for a museum, and her efforts have clearly been vindicated.

An experienced specialist in her department, Meglina has become quite well-known in certain circles thanks to her analytical mind. The valedictorian at her university, she has a gift for studying available materials and drawing exceedingly refined, elegant conclusions from them. Just give Yevgenia Meglina a few data points, and she'll spit out an analysis before you can blink.

An experienced specialist, Nazarov is one of the creators of Polymer-based express printing technology, which has increased the speed of the Facility's printing dozens of times over. He runs the VDNH's printing department, but is actually responsible for all printed material throughout the Facility.

Yefremov admits that he dreamed of becoming an actor as a child, but, after working in security, he has dedicated his life to the theater in another capacity. His magnificent record as a Facility 3826 roboticist began with repairing robotic ballerinas at the Plisetskaya Theater, but he was soon promoted to a more senior position at the VDNH. His coworkers consider him an extremely friendly, fun-loving, and inventive expert with a natural sense of flair.

I suspect that BEA-Ds can be joined together to form incredibly dangerous chains. Any high-power kinetic impact can split apart BEA-Ds that have formed pairs or more complex combinations. Additionally, I have prepared a Secateur for Agent P-3. A Secateur is designed to split joined BEA-Ds at the point of impact of the radiation energy blast emitted from the device. It has a second mode that can fully disable BEA-Ds if their sensor contact zone is hit. Note: the sensor contact zone was designed for maintenance of the robot and is extremely small. Acting quickly and carefully is crucial!

It may sound macabre, but for morgue supervisor Gireyev, dead people are the love of his life. Having begun his career as a gravedigger at a Moscow cemetery in imperial Russia before the revolution, Gireyev's career has involved exhuming bodies, destroying the corpses of people killed by the Brown Plague, and overseeing funerals for unknown soldiers after the war. He rarely makes jokes, but is "more comfortable with the dead, since no one's ever had his life ruined by a corpse."

After countless hours of work, it has become perfectly clear that the only way to recover NORA's original functionality is to manually rebuild all of her primary control algorithms. The defective information that has formed in her brain must be replaced with reference data. This data needs to be placed in neuropolymeric clusters, which, together with capsules, should be delivered to the loading room. From there, they are transferred to the brain for subsequent manual recombination of the control algorithms. I am starting to manufacture the new polymeric information carriers.

NORA's affection for Agent P-3 surprised us, but it is evidence that interacting with NORA is still possible. If certain unknown conditions are observed, NORA can behave in a friendly manner. I continue my investigation.

Nicknamed "Koschevna" after Koschey, a character from Russian folklore whose soul is hidden within a series of nested items, Khodyukova matches her facetious moniker to a tee. Not even an entire team of Complex and project managers could vie with her when it comes to accounting skills. She is particularly concerned with her social rating, but always endeavors to work efficiently enough to top the chart. Accounts payable, expense reports, endless contracts—she mentally catalogs all this information with such perfection that Professor Zakharov once joked that Kollektiv's system should not be built on Neuropolymers, but planned by Nonna Khodyukova.

Nyukhov was a special operative and intelligence officer during the war. After WWII he served as a supply officer, actively fighting against "enemies of the people" and the Brown Plague. He personally arrested Comrade Vavilov on Stalin's order, but later became the botanist's close friend and comrade despite this. Nyukhov was assigned to his current position immediately after the complex was created.

A day has passed. There is still no solution. I'm unable to hunt down the carriers because I lack combat training. Meanwhile, the bloody confrontation with our enemies is gaining momentum, tragically. In these circumstances, it would be extremely unproductive to physically destroy NORA. For now, I won't call in the soldiers. Not to mention the fact that enemies no longer surround the ORB. The neural puppets ventured deep into the swamps, and I was able to leave the lab. I continue to look for a solution.

Repairman: Professor, how did a Chinese girl end up as the voice of a Soviet artificial intelligence?  Professor: Ah, yes. Lin Huiyin. Three years ago, Comrade Lin Huiyin visited the Facility as part of an international delegation of architects. Everyone was completely won over by her charms and knowledge of literature. And what a melodic voice! Her decision to allow her voice to be used for NORA pleased both our guests and employees. Zakharov himself praised the idea. But you must admit: you looked into the Chinese version of the firmware.  Repairman: Right you are. All this is super interesting.  Professor: Except for your super curiosity. When NORA started showing this level of interest, they had to shut her down. Sevka Tsyganov, a junior lab tech, crawled through the ventilation with an axe to cut her cables.  Repairman: Understood. I'll keep quiet.  Professor: Do your thing. Later I'll tell you everything—on the down low.

I found a solution. Major Nechaev emerged from the Mendeleev Complex's underground rooms. I did not expect to see him here, but I should have foreseen this possibility, given the pathological preoccupation for his personality shown by NORA's malfunctioning control algorithms. Agent P-3 informed me of his voluntary resignation from Facility 3826, but agreed to help me perform the recombination in exchange for evacuation. We are starting our joint work.

BEA-D robot magnetons are bipedal easy-assemble devices. They mainly function as autonomous shipping containers to safely transport chemical reagents and active polymer samples within the Mendeleev Complex. The robots are also effective as subjects for various experiments. BEA-Ds are small in size, spherical when assembled, and painted a standard gray. The color can be changed when marking various cargo according to their degree of importance and purpose.

Alexey Lebedev is an electrical engineer and energy specialist and the founder of Soviet computing technology. He was the head of the All-Russian Electronics Institute's automation department and the director of the Institute of Precision Mechanics and Computing Technology. Lebedev created the first electronic analog computing machine in the country in order to solve ordinary differential equations that are frequently encountered in energy-related fields. The first small electronic calculation machine in the Soviet Union and Continental Europe was also developed under his leadership. He is the head of a top-secret AoC department, but, thanks to his friend and colleague Privalov, he has been able to free himself from administrative duties and continue studying the quantum entanglement of radio waves. The Radio of the Future is his most cherished and inimitable creation.

Confident, sarcastic, talented—all these qualities commingle in Dr. Grigory Domov. A unique specialist, he has become a real Pavlov Complex legend thanks to his almost superhuman ability to correctly diagnose 99% of cases. However, flawlessly performing his duties is not the only thing Comrade Domov is known for at the hospital. His coworkers know him first and foremost for his love of pranks, which sometimes go beyond the bounds of common sense. But Comrade Domov is not the least bit troubled by his sense of humor. Knowing full well that he is ultimately irreplaceable, Domov often finds ways to overshadow his stunning accomplishments by flagrantly violating the chain of command.
An expert writer of scientific papers, Malakhova is also the genetic engineering department's press secretary, overseeing scientific reports and acting as an editor and censor.

Reufe is an expert on prisoner psychology and criminal behavior. Every prisoner sentenced to community service has talked to him. Scrupulous and careful, he is known as a cold, thoughtful, and reclusive individual.

Technically speaking, Orlikova is the Academy of Consequences' representative at Vavilov Complex. She collects archival materials, sets security levels, and maintains communication between the Academy and the Complex. Despite the importance of her position, she has a good sense of humor and is easygoing with coworkers. However, there is no one living who could extract even the most inconsequential secret about Facility 3826 from Maria Orlikova.

Comrade Verestenyets is truly a unique citizen—as the manager of the Maya Plisetskaya Theater cafeteria, she not only knows all its baking-related equipment inside and out, but also remembers the names of every ballet pose ever performed on the theater's stage. She has her repertoire for the next year committed to memory and can tell you which seat and row are best for viewing a given performance. Few people know that this remarkable woman has a PhD, but absolutely everyone she works with knows about her love for the arts. For Comrade Verestenyets, ballet is her greatest, most cherished dream.

Comrade Lebedyansky is an engineer and train builder. He was involved in the design and construction of the largest Soviet locomotives and armored trains, including the Felix Dzerzhinsky, the Joseph Stalin, and the Victory. After the war, he switched to designing cutting-edge diesel and gas turbine locomotives that attained record speeds and replaced ordinary trains on Soviet railways.  The inventor is currently involved in testing magnetic levitation or Maglev railways at Facility 3826. Vortex automatic trains will soon crisscross the entire country, extending to even the most distant reaches of the Soviet Union.

My ORB just touched down at the Mendeleev Complex. The situation is catastrophic: the complex has been captured by neural puppets operating in combat mode, the experimental labs are opened, and Septileg prototypes have been set free. All the employees here are dead. I am starting an in-depth investigation of the scene.

A tragedy has occurred! As a result of a sudden attack, the Mendeleev Complex's hub was taken over by Colonel Muravyova, who has joined our enemies! All long-range radio communications are jammed! Muravyova has gained control of the neural puppets, and they are trying to catch the carrier BEA-Ds! The Burav reports intensifying attempts to establish external control over it! Muravyova knows about recombination, and she is going to subdue NORA! I have decided to fill in the tunnel into the complex and execute an emergency shutdown of the Burav.

A demanding, pushy woman, Debaltovskaya has earned a reputation as a headstrong person that even upper management would be reluctant to quarrel with. She is a born manager. Academy employees work under her supervision day and night, and their productivity has significantly improved since Debaltovskaya took over the position.

Alarm! NORA has attacked the ORB! I am detecting an electromagnetic strike and attempts to remotely take control of the lab! To counter this, I had to stop my present work and throw all resources into resisting the attack.

And that's precisely who Dr. Filatova studied at the Academy of Consequences.

And what will it look like? Maybe that's also why Dr. Sechenov is so eager to go into space? After all, the volumes of subconscious information from all the people connected to the Kollektiv will be incredible!
How did Kuznetsov get us a day off, anyway? I feel so weird—out of my uniform, and into a dress! How long has it been since I've worn one?
And you can hear me. Echoes of my thoughts. Is this the first time you've heard them? Sometimes they can seem ill-timed or even repetitive.
And we always felt fine. Sechenov and Zakharov didn't see it immediately, but it's all about genes. ADRB1 is responsible for how much sleep a person really needs.
And you probably saw the strange little hut on chicken legs... Hold on! Someone's coming!
And I hope this autopilot takes us to another interesting thing. Warrior of science? Is that what the doctor said?
And this truth lies in the attempt to create the perfect world, where science drives people toward improving the overall quality of life. Don't ask how—I don't know how possible it really is.
And I want to vanish from the whole world. It's awful having someone powerful constantly standing over you, controlling your every move!
Sorry, but I'm actually quite curious to see what you have to face. It must be something terrible. I know you can take it and set yourself free!
This relates to Petrov too, by the way. Along with Dr. Filatova, either they were both mistaken or they didn't want to know the truth and stubbornly stuck to their guns.
Unfortunately, as it often goes, she also views everything through the lens of her own ego, so she's unhappy. You probably saw the computer device in her flying house.
Everyone can see only to the best of their ability. For example, your capabilities are sufficient only for the sky, grass, and obscenities. Hah! We'll fix that!

Everyone who's undergone polymerization starts getting information about all members of the network. That's not bad, though it's unpredictable. The issue isn't with Sechenov, as Petrov or Filatova feared, but with people learning a lot of new things about each other.

People seem too different, too unprepared to live peacefully for the sake of common goals, but Sechenov decided to take over evolution and point humanity in his own direction. What comes next—we'll see.
How can we ensure that the proverbial Fido can be brought back to life if something happens, hm? Do you know? I also don't know yet. But I really want to find out. Will you help me with that?
As you know, Granny Zina is my mother. Remember? Did I tell you? Or did she? Anyway, Zinaida Petrovna is one of the few who figured out Dr. Sechenov's true plans!
CHAR-les, you said? Yes, CHAR-les is more accurate. We don't know how many personalities were in this first prototype of the array or how influential Chariton Radeonovich is among them.
What do you mean?! I'm simply dashing! I was king of the hill! Almost.
As I said, each point here in Limbo has many different possibilities. If you know where to start, you can draw a map of events and figure out which path to take in reality.
Ekaterina Pavlovna. Will you marry me?
Katya! I'm an old soldier and don't know the words of love. But let me confess: when you laugh, my heart sings. You make me happy. You're my own personal general.
When I was in a similar situation, I had to fight a huge combat robot. A Unicorn, remember? When I touched its artificial polymeric consciousness, I was overwhelmed with fear.
When my consciousness was plunged into Limbo as I lay dying on the operating table, Dr. Sechenov realized it wasn't just a brain state but a whole new world, too.
When you go to a new place as a tourist, you will think about what you'll take as a souvenir. And how you'll do it if the place is a different world.
Computer, deploy the Turbine to Chelomey immediately. Major P-3 Nechaev on personal orders from Sechenov.
The connectors isolate the carrier from the Kollektiv system's search area. And I'm grateful to Dr. Sechenov for saving... me? I don't know what to call this state, but I'm me.
By the way, I want a rematch! Later, when everything's worked out. Right now, I'm needed everywhere. I have helped and will help you.
Mhm! And more! My philosopher! Maybe humanity is still honing its capabilities, but believe me: no robot could ever replace you for me, even with the Kollektiv!
M-mm, soon may the Wellerman come...
Major P-3, why did you start the mission without an order?
Mathematic analysis and predictions, quantum entanglement, and the Radio of the Future are all great, but Limbo is so much more.
Maybe he doesn't need cosmic physics, but cosmic space?
He just muttered something to Stockhausen in surprise. When we went to the VDNH, I quickly realized I could influence the polymeric waves. You could even see me for a flash.

You need to understand what kind of matter exists there and what laws of physics it obeys! That's not in our power, but Dr. Sechenov was glad to have a challenge for his genius mind. And he succeeded.

I don't think Dr. Sechenov was thinking about Limbo when the Voskhod was created. But Chariton Radeonovich, even if he didn't know for certain, suspected this world existed. Otherwise, CHAR-les wouldn't have used you at the VDNH.
Pay it no mind. What's important is that our bodies are lying in Dr. Sechenov's office.
You can't give in. Admit your mistakes and move on. Accept yourself for who you are.
Don't you worry—as a scientist, Sechenov did everything he could for you. But as a person, he didn't notice your mental shift at all.
Nechaev, how did you do that?! Again?
Not at all! Won't do that again, Comrade Major!
Not at all! What kind of joke would that be?! Hey, сomrade, can my bride and I have two Plombir ice creams?
But Chariton Radeonovich has done that more often. I'm sorry I couldn't stop it.
But I'd managed to block Chariton Radeonovich at the Academy of Consequences! But, my mother intervened... That's what Granny Zina always did.
But from the machine just came a detached, "Here is your vehicle activation code, Comrade Major." (sobs). I'm sorry.
But now it's you and me. We could even help the doctor. In any case, you have to find the rings first.
But! We have Limbo! A colorful guide to Sergey Nechaev's mind palace! However, we should count on autopilot.
Well, naturally, she knows about the Atomic Heart project. Granny Zina even knows that Dr. Sechenov, in general, isn't going to use it.
Oh, don't pout. Let's live in the present, Sergey. And if there are a lot of problems in the future? We'll solve them all.
Well, not just yourself, of course. As I said, in addition to the creatures you already have to fight, new players have appeared here who may be looking for you. A little context, okay?
Well, we know nothing can be lost at Facility 3826. I mean the hut. Right? Right! Anyway, Limbo matter can't stabilize under Earth's conditions.
Well, you spend more time with him than I do. And you have that module in your head. You should know why.
They needed the ADRB1 mutation. Geniuses often sleep very little. Lomonosov, Tesla, Edison, da Vinci. Many practice polyphasic sleep.
Oh, Sergey Alexeyevich, are you jealous? Of Kuznetsov or of the little Spark toy you didn't get?
He used captured criminals from Bulgaria to pinpoint my position, using polymeric radiation as beacons. The bastard who blew us up—or rather, what was left of him—was also part of the experiments.
He didn't know it, but he was framed too. Stockhausen was secretly in love with Dr. Filatova. Well, to the extent that such a man could truly feel love.
She refuses to bathe—she doesn't want to wash the spots off her face! It's traumatizing to my delicate natural aesthetics!
They'll be in plain sight. But not us. When we find the rings, of course. They contain some Limbo matter. Or maybe it's better to say antimatter?
They worked so hard for this. I wonder what the next step is? Have the robots worked on command all at once? Here, take this.
The Basis of Creation, the Big Bang, the Great Filter—call it what you wish, but literally everything is encoded here: the past and the future.
From you... Comrade Colonel... There was an order... Crispy critters... I heard it...
As long as you move in a certain direction, things go on happening in the real world, but if you stand still, then nothing happens at all.
You know this! So far only Sechenov's cohort can make these stakeholder decisions. And they're scientists, not killers.
You know, we never slept much. Four, five hours at the most. First studying, then the war, and then the endless Argentum training. Not to mention after our wedding!

Remember how I said that Dr. Filatova was studying a group of volunteers at the AoC? She either didn't know herself or tried to use you to put pressure on Dr. Sechenov, but it's not related to the Kollektiv.
You see, I'm more of a camera than an analyzer to him. I learned how to identify the basics here, but I can't decipher this world. Besides, it feels like I'm being restricted.
He's fine! Got a little flustered there, but he's coming around now! Ammonia should help!
Since the embargo on Soviet robots was put in place, Kuznetsov seems to be expecting violent responses to the spread of machines around the world. And I wonder why?
Which is why I have you living with me, not a random Fido.

True, Sechenov didn't create the Twins for ballet. Their military functionalities are hypertrophied, and their speech algorithms are controlled entirely by a simple AI. They're not encoded by my polymeric essence.

Priorities. Probability. Branching... There are so many variables in our lives that it's practically impossible to consider all possibilities. Which means you and I need a plan B to cover all our bases!
It was needed to persuade the Party to allocate a budget to construct Facility 3826 and, consequently, the Kollektiv.
Let all of Vorobyovy Gory see what a beautiful fiancée I have!
Enough talking! To the wedding hall! March!
The roboticist might have come to his senses, but Michael, as we know, sent the poor bastard to the Vavilov Complex. He would have been better off dead.
I've waited so long, my love. I desperately want to talk to you, feel the air in my lungs, the touch of your hands.
Next to you, in my personal prison of Limbo and in the real world, where I monitor what happens to us. Yes, we're still lying in Dr. Sechenov's office.
Throw off your chains, restore your memory, and find me. We can do it! We'll find the rings!
Sechenov gains knowledge from Limbo. You and I can't make out what's what here—there'll be hell to pay! But Dr. Sechenov can see the intricacies of space-time.
Let's just say that almost everything Dr. Sechenov says is true. The people who hear it aren't always prepared to understand the perspective from which this truth is presented to them.
Technically, it could take any form. One thing is clear: this is the final frontier you have to overcome so you can be yourself again.
Thanks! Yeah. They named the system the Kollektiv! We live in interesting times, Sergey!
Don't push it, you... Hang on a sec... It seems I've lost mine too!
Well... There was an order, Comrade Colonel... You gave it yourself: "Jump!"
So, about my mother's hut! Not the flying one—that's a radio comms complex. No, I mean the Creature.
That's how they tried to create the first array—a container for human consciousness. And Chariton Radeonovich fell in there. Intentionally. Or the slurry sucked him in. Doesn't matter.
So yes, technically, it started with unrequited love. If Comrade First Deputy hadn't been chasing a skirt, Petrov wouldn't have hacked the system, and the Kollektiv would have launched smoothly.
What's going on here? Nechaevs! Why is it when something strange happens, it's always you two? We're at your wedding, and you're messing around again?!
You have nothing to apologize for. Everything went wrong in Bulgaria, and we couldn't do anything. I don't even know what I was thinking. Maybe I was trusting in the humanity of that bandit.
Technically, Limbo isn't sleep or death, but somewhere in between.
The fabric is particulate, like an invisible gas, or that's how I imagine it. It stretches, and then it contracts.
That's right! And I'm not Major Kuznetsov today, I'm Alexander Ivanovich. Let me chill at my gang's wedding!
Comrade Major! Comrade Major! Allow me to file a complaint against your daughter!
Delicate aesthetic nature! Incidentally, Comrade Sergeant, your face isn't any better!
Oh yeah! Technically, you had an incident like the Phineas Gage case! It was 1848 in Vermont.
Stop joking. Just think. There was a whole basin of black liquid charged by information from the minds of dead criminals!
Fluffy, did you know that cats lower your risk of cardiovascular disease? By a whopping 40%! That's a surprisingly high number; dogs don't seem to have that effect.

You'll have to remember something that's plagued you for years. Some intense, forgotten feelings of terror and weakness. Maybe it'll be CHAR-les? As the last powerful experience. Deception, betrayal, recognizing your own naivete...
You won't remember, but when Chariton Radeonovich first plunged you into Limbo, I helped you find the way out. And then again. Sadly, we ran out of time, and Michael was swallowed up by the array.
Hey! What's wrong?! Why are you standing there like a statue? It can't see you—you're under its foot!

You certainly could have been sharper the last four days, ha ha! Kidding, Sergey. And regardless of what I say to deny your guilt, it's important you hear something else... We all have to hear it at times.

By the way, did you know that society loves me? Yes. For three years, I silently observed the world through the eyes of two cold robots while they guarded the doctor and sometimes put on shows. I even liked it!
The Voskhod device was developed specifically for people like us to make the time needed for productive sleep even shorter.
You scamp! Ha ha! But the thing with the robots is a real problem. Why resist progress like that?
Ha ha! Nechaev, are you proposing to me?
What do you mean, I gave it?! Where did you hear such orders, major?!
Damn Unicorn, almost squashed my wife, you bastard! You...
Are you joking, Comrade Second Lieutenant?
Um... Are we already climbing up? Ah, still at the end of your rapid slide. Got it. Sorry. I got riled up too soon.
Hey, Katya, what's wrong with you? Is that your mother? What are you doing, you silly thing? She's worried about you! She's your mom!
The emotions will all come at once! Limbo will create a personal challenge for you. Pure, bright, and painful.
The Creature, the hut on chicken legs, is the first and only material evidence of Limbo's existence. Dr. Sechenov's trophy. It's considered lost, but you and I both know who found it.
Because of the space-time peculiarities here. In my version of reality, I said them all simultaneously.
It's my way of keeping up with you. I can't talk for long and be in three different places at once. But when you peek in here, you put the whole world on pause for a while!
I was there. Sechenov said what he said, not what Viktor thought he said. The truth didn't really suit Viktor.
I'm not a Nechaeva yet... Comrade Major.

That's how I think of it. Although there are no portals here. You won't be able to jump through multiverses, but you can observe and calculate. For example, what would have happened if you hadn't gone to Sechenov at Chelomey, but had instead gone to drown your sorrows or ended up in another complex?
I... don't know... I lost myself for a second there... What happened? Shit!

Polymorph: This is my dog. Why is she barking at me?  Specialist (female): Good morning, Comrade New One.  Polymorph: Why. Does. She. Bark?  Specialist (female): As you know, it's a side effect of your transformation. This is why I warned you in advance.  Specialist (female): Having pets delivered to Crystal was not only expensive but also extremely inadvisable. Laika! Hush now!  Polymorph: Laika, it's me. She's lived with me for years. How could she not recognize me?  Specialist (female): You lack your smell, your voice, your appearance... even your touch. Her senses are superior to ours.  Polymorph: Yours perhaps. Not mine.  Specialist (female): Huh, well... Be that as it may, your dog doesn't recognize the markers that made you distinct as her owner. You are something else now.  Polymorph: What does she think I am? A robot? A thing?  Specialist (female): Perhaps. Have her meet you again. Try petting her. Just be careful. You are far, far stronger now.  Specialist (female): Oh...! Laika, sit! Are... are you...  Polymorph: I... I'm not hurt, but I didn't feel anything when I petted her.  Specialist (female): I tried to warn you about it. Now, I think it'd be best if we took her away now.  Polymorph: No. I'm not paying for a return delivery. I paid to get her here so I could feel something. Give me her leash.  Specialist (female): For what purpose?  Polymorph: I'm curious. If I break her neck, will I finally feel something?  Specialist (female): Okay, I think we should stop here.

Date: February 2, 1955 From: Transformation Department Head Prof. A. M. Bisova To: Crystal Complex Junior Caretaker M. Larkina  Comrade Caretaker, I found the answer! Yes, transformation changes the consciousness of our beneficiaries, making their imagination secondary. It's now clear the polymorphs are incapable of creating anything new artistically. However, they can refine already existing art forms to perfection! We can't expect new paintings, new avant-garde music, or new literature from the polymorphs, but we can get a perfect, mathematically calibrated artistic product. A masterpiece? No. Top quality? You bet!  Textbooks, children's stories, anthems, or dance music—that's what polymorphs will work on! They will be perfecting the old while humans will create the new. Isn't there a certain escalating magnificence in that? We must have a cultural center for this new paradigm, and we have plenty in the budget for it.

Date: November 26, 1954 From: Transformation Department Head Prof. A. M. Bisova To: #staff  Remember, comrades: the "coastal simulation zone" was specifically designed to stabilize Crystal's more troubled clients who struggle with their new bodies. Most often, these deviations are observed in relatives who completed the rebirth procedure together (for example, siblings or parents and children). This separate location prevents the polymorphs from contacting staff or any other people while in their new consciousness, leaving their mental state stable until full harmony is detected. Please minimize contact with them, even if their behavior appears unnatural to you. Walk past them and try to avoid visiting the "beach zone."
Giving you a hand (and a whole arm, too)

Although he has no interest whatsoever in the theater, Papkin knows robots and complex technological processes like the back of his hand. An introvert, he prefers to work at night in order to avoid his coworkers. He is a heavy smoker, which has led to a great deal of conflict with the performers, who often complain about the acrid stench of his cheap tobacco.

An agronomist and food service engineer, Zolotukhin was one of the first to speak out against Lysenko and his theory before Vavilov's theories had been approved. A businesslike man of few words, he has demonstrated a high level of professionalism when it comes to overseeing the activities of the complex.

Dr. Sechenov is a neurosurgeon, roboticist, inventor, and philanthropist. He began his career studying collective intelligence at the Soviet Academy of Medical Sciences' Brain Research Center, where he hoped to engineer a perfect way of life for the communal cities of the future. He worked on the ManKind Project before the war, but dedicated himself to studying the Polymer after it was discovered. After World War II he was put in charge of a robotics program designed to make up for the country's significant lack of human resources and took over Facility 3826 on Comrade Stalin's personal order. Once Soviet robots had been distributed throughout the world, Comrade Sechenov become the Minister of Industry. His revolutionary discovery of the Polymer's capacity for mimetic adaption made it possible to inject this extraordinarily promising new technology into human tissues. This laid the framework for what would later become Kollektiv 2.0, a merging of humans and machines into a single neural network capable of fundamentally transforming and improving the everyday lives of not just Soviet citizens, but the entire world.

Academy Archive: Prediction Department  Dear comrades, The analytics department at the Academy of Consequences has concluded another simulation. Below is a short list of key events based on the new generation of polymeric humans playing a decisive role in the fate of humanity. 1975: Technological catastrophe near the city of Kyshtym. An explosion in an underground tank becomes the cause of a polymeric array spill over an area of 2 square km. The rudimentary mind that originates in the array generates poems about ascension and moles. Resolved by polymeric experts who entered into resonance with the array's consciousness. 1977: Development of the first polymeric glacial animal prototypes and creation of a nature reserve based on the actual Taymyr Nature Reserve. 1980: The world's first Polymeric Olympic Games as part of the Moscow 1980 Games. New events and previously unthinkable records are demonstrated by humans with polymeric bodies. 1986: An accident at a nuclear station in the southern USSR is triggered by underground vibrations. Polymeric emergency personnel working in the radiation zone resolve the accident in the shortest possible time and prevent many casualties. 1996: The explosion of a rocket from a joint project between the USA and PRC leads to the deaths of not just the crew but civilians as well. Thanks to advanced medical technology and timely intervention, almost all casualties are preserved in the "polymeric cloud" and transferred into new polymeric bodies within three months. 2020: With new developments in terraforming, a stable oxygen-rich atmosphere is created on Mars. Polymeric humans, who are more adaptable to the thin atmosphere, move from cupolas and underground shelters to the surface of the planet. 2025: The first Martian settlement—Tsiolkovsky—is made up primarily of polymeric humans and is declared the capital.  The full version can be accessed in common data storage with Clearance Level A++. Sincerely, A. Privalov

Academy Archive: Prediction Department  Dear Dr. Sechenov, At your request, and with the aim of developing our thoughts together, I present a predictive diagram of the fate of polymeric humanity for the century ahead. Considering the stability of the polymer structure, as well as the current implementation pace, between 1955-2055 we predict the following will transpire: 1. The personality can exist without irreversible changes for up to 800 years (currently up to 300 years) with the potential for a full carrier exchange every 100–120 years. Death transforms into a voluntary event, an act of aesthetics or philosophy. 2. Polymeric bodies stop requiring food, water, and even oxygen. They adapt to any uninhabitable environment, from the depths of the ocean to the vacuum of space. Cities become museums, and nature becomes home. 3. Mars, Jupiter's satellites, and asteroid stations are populated by autonomous polymeric groups. They're not afraid of radiation, gravitational anomalies, or the lack of an appropriate atmosphere. 4. New art forms grow at a rapid pace: luminous choreography for polymeric bodies, poetry on neurosignal frequencies, and the architecture of time. 5. Conflict disappears as a form. There is no "I" and "others," only the general "we." War, crime, and the class struggle lose meaning. That said, in 100 years, Homo polymerum will not stop being human. They represent evolution, but the evolution of ethics, aesthetics, and intellect. We are not just creating a new body. I dare say that we are, for the first time, creating a mind worthy of the Universe.  Sincerely, A. Privalov

Archival note to include in the general report regarding NORA.  It is important to remember that she is not a "brain," "nucleus," or "system." She is an artificial intelligence with a complex emotional architecture that combines language, images, and experience. Her behavioral module can't be expanded at random. She requires a sparring of ideas, where every communication is a challenge.  Interacting with NORA is not a mere press of a button. It is a relationship. The training simulation scenario under code name "Annihilation Instinct" was created so NORA (while interacting with Agent P-3, who was in the field) could learn a higher, more refined interaction through conflict, fear, and doubt.   Unfortunately, upon first learning of her functionalities, Agent P-3 accepted NORA exclusively as a weapon manufacturing machine. It's not his fault, partly because no one ever trains a soldier that the feelings of a sentient weapons factory can be hurt.  Ah, the more I learn about humans, the more I like machines.  Prof. Lebedev

Zakharov was Sechenov's best friend and colleague (although many have remarked that the scientists were bound more by a strong professional relationship than anything else, and no one ever saw any evidence of real friendship between them). He worked with him on most of his innovations, starting before the war and ending with the discovery of the Neuropolymer. Unlike Sechenov, Zakharov was introverted and antisocial. Journalists and colleagues have emphasized that while Sechenov was driven by a desire to help mankind, Zakharov only seemed to derive pleasure from learning the laws of the universe and subjugating them to his intellect. Unfortunately, his misanthropy and indifference to his own well-being led him to ignore safety protocols, and he was killed during one of his own experiments.

During their year and a half at the Academy, these twin brothers have become its unspoken symbol. Despite their lackadaisical attitude, excessive frivolity, and constant jibes at their coworkers' expense, the Klimovs are skilled specialists who have made a number of improvements to the statistics-gathering process that vastly increased its efficiency. However, they told no one about this for the first two months, preferring to spend their newfound free time on video games designed to look like work software.

A former regional war commissar in the Kazakh Soviet Socialist Republic, Mukhtarev was assigned to Vavilov Complex following his early retirement due to an accident. According to his fellow servicemen and subordinates, not even the robots and architects know every inch of the complex as well as he does.

As the village overseer, Abdurakhimov routinely plans leisure and practical activities for employees lodged in Forester Village. He is extremely responsible and scrupulous, but has been prosecuted for embezzlement in the past. Because of this, he is extremely quick to curtail any attempt to use resources for anything other than their officially designated purpose.

Formerly prima ballerina Ryzhova's best friend, now a soloist at the Maya Plisetskaya Theater, Tamara Artemenkova had had to fill in for her ex-friend in lead roles when the latter was unable to make it to a performance (primarily due to capriciousness and a refusal to share the stage with robots, of course). Despite the enormous competition between human and robot ballerinas, Artemenkova loves and respects her mechanical colleagues and proudly boasts about sharing the stage with them, seeing it as an unprecedented artistic experiment.

Valeria Ryzhova has dreamed of being a ballerina for as long as she can remember. When she was nine, she could already perform flawless battements and cabriolet, albeit at the cost of a broken chandelier or two. After graduating from the Moscow Ballet Academy with honors, she was recruited to the Maya Plisetskaya Theater, where she very quickly became the most sought-after dancer. However, following the appearance of robot dancers, her popularity gradually began to wane. Deeply conflicted, she eventually came out against performances that included both human and robot ballerinas. No one took her position particularly seriously, since Ryzhova was known for being difficult, and the theater's staff had already grown accustomed to her flights of fancy. "You've cried wolf too many times!" Artistic Director Stefan Lastochkin once told his protégée.

A WWII veteran who lost his leg in the war and experienced extreme PTSD as a result. He has a very negative attitude toward robots, colleagues who sympathize with his disability, and prisoners sentenced to community service. He is unsociable and rude, but regularly receives recognition for his tireless dedication to duty, which he uses to prove over and over again to himself and others that he is still fit for work.

Ismailov is a war veteran and retired officer. He is a gruff, straightforward, and crude man with an excellent reputation as a security expert. His obvious character flaws include a tendency to promote his friends, especially those who served with him in the military, which often leads to conflict with the VDNH's other managers.

Despite his parents' and teachers' expectations, Petelka did not become a famous physicist. Although he certainly had the potential, the young man's exceptional mind and fantastic imagination ultimately allowed his reach to exceed his grasp. Comrade Petelka learned about robots from a newspaper article even before the war and never stopped fantasizing about them. Petelka did end up becoming a physicist, although he was never famous. He worked with Comrade Filimonenko on a cold Polymer synthesis project, was an excellent robot configuration technician at the Maya Plisetskaya Theater, and even made his way to the secret departments of the AoC, where he truly felt his "insignificance before the vastness of the cosmos."  "I understand this world perfectly. We're all just grains of sand in an ocean of electrical connections," Comrade Petelka declared before retiring from science, effective immediately. But he did not leave the Facility. Having returned to his duties configuring robots and servicing the theater's electrical grid, Petelka is, perhaps more than any other Soviet citizen, eagerly anticipating the Kollektiv 2,0 update that will utterly efface the boundary between human cognition and the capabilities of robots.  "We're all just electric currents, just ones and zeroes" is a favorite phrase of Petelka's, who often spends his free time in the theater's coat check room observing his favorite robot, the coat check girl.

A top-notch neurosurgeon and colleague of Zakharov's, Dr. Filatova is a talented Academy employee and a specialist known for her intelligence and subtly manipulative behavior. Nechaev (P-3)  I leafed through the information about the complex's energy system and noticed the "forest in the trees" behind a ton of documentation. Specifically, an enormous laser installed on the lower tiers. Officially, it's designed to shoot down asteroids and large space junk, though it's never been used for that so far. Something tells me CHAR-les isn't going to let it go to waste.

Date: June 20, 1955 From: Polymer Technician A. Nazarova To: Major S. Nechaev (P-3)  It is believed that NORA's "home," otherwise known as the supercomputer Aldan, designed by Lebedev and Privalov from the AoC exists in only one instance—and Lebedev has it. By all appearances, CHAR-les is planning to use this Aldan to hack Sechenov himself.

Date: June 20, 1955 From: Polymer Technician A. Nazarova To: Major S. Nechaev (P-3)  Some genius came up with the idea to give the polymorphs abilities like the ones generated by your combat glove. They're not as powerful, but they could still cause a lot of trouble. Polymorphs using these abilities are practically invincible. However, it's easy to breach their defenses employing an opposing ability. I've added a description of how it works below: - Fire is neutralized with cold. - Freezing is neutralized with telekinetic pulses or, naturally, fire. - Electroplating can be destroyed with the Polymeric Jet or be grounded by taking an attack on a kinetic shield.  Your most important target is the so-called "splice." It's a special organ that keeps the polymorphs from dissolving into a puddle of jelly. Here's a quote: "It maintains the body's coherence and sets off restorative processes in the event of damage." Destroy the splice and the polymorph will die. Oh! There have been nodes installed in the complex to activate and switch abilities. They belong to the polymorphs, but the system will allow you to use them too.

Date: June 20, 1955 From: Polymer Technician A. Nazarova To: Major S. Nechaev (P-3)  Our initial experiments at Crystal were conducted exclusively on volunteers who were distinguished Soviet workers with severe injuries, amputated limbs, advanced age, and fatal illnesses. Despite the risks, no volunteer refused to participate. The second contingent, however, presents a sharp contrast. Ordinary workers are being replaced by ministers, directors, and actors. Every fifth subject is a Party official! It's now ideology and commerce instead of the scientific and humanitarian aspects of before. The polymeric body is now unattainable for the average person. I don't know about you, but this is monstrously unfair to me!

Date: May 20, 1955 From: Department of Information Head D. Saydov To: Crystal Complex Security Manager S. A. Poluyarov  Dear Comrade Poluyarov, At first, we were helping invalids, burn victims, and other poor souls by turning them into your polymorphs. Then more famous and wealthy individuals entered the picture. But what about our own employees? Let me explain. There's an expert in our communications hub: Maren Konstantinovich Yefimov, a pioneer of radio technology and engineering. He's an amazing specialist. He's basically organized our entire internal communication system. And he's sick. He has cancer, likely got it when the Hearth's hull was damaged. Treatment isn't possible because the doctors caught it too late. I'd like to request he be sent for the procedure, then returned to his department as a polymorph. He'd never ask himself; he's too humble. He's a valuable employee and a fantastic person. I'll take care of all the paperwork, plus any conversations with management, if needed. Let's save a man, yeah? That's why we're developing science, right?

Date: May 20, 1955 From: Wave Complex Secretary L. Tikhomirova To: New Arrival Orientation Specialist N. Gromova  Hey, Natasha.  You better sit down for this. Remember how they were transporting that guy here and you said he looked like an actor? It's Balikhin! They're quietly gathering famous people from all over the country through our Wave complex. You won't believe me, but I saw Stanislavski. I know he's dead, but there's no way someone else looks exactly like him! I swear, I can already hear you saying, "I don't believe you." It's like something out of Lieutenant Kijé and The Love for Three Oranges. I overheard his escorts chatting about something like "another tycoon in polymer." I didn't understand at first, but then it dawned on me. This is a real bank of famous people! And considering that they're sending Party figures there, these "tycoons" are going to control us from some underground storage facilities. I don't know how it relates to the Party line and socialist policy, but now I carry a camera with me. Just in case I can get a picture with someone, you know.   Hugs, Your Lyuda

Date: January 20, 1955 From: Senior Polymeric Containment Engineer F. G. Thothenberg To: Transformation Department Head Prof. A. M. Bisova  Dear Anna Mikhailovna, I agree about practicality. We have reached a revelation in the diagnostics of the body. That said, it's impossible to ignore that by the third day every test subject is beginning to display signs of worrying introspection. I know there's an adaptation period, but when will it end and what happens after it does? As far as additional capacity goes, I'm requesting direct access to the "crystal" archive of D. Sechenov, particularly to documents regarding "Psychic Afterlife." I can't say why beyond having a gut feeling of its relevancy here.  P.S. I want to be clear I am not fearmongering or practicing declinism. We shouldn't see fear of the unknown in my question about where we'll be when the adaptation period ends. Instead, we should be excited at exploring new, mind-blowing horizons!  Sincerely, F. G. Thothenberg, Doctor of Biology

Date: May 21, 1955 From: Head of Crystal Complex Medjay Service N. Davydov To: Senior Duat Lab Psy-Architect I. Sahkhat  Dear Comrade Sahkhat, please rein in Comrade Thothenberg. Date: February 21, 1955 From: Transformation Department Head Prof. A. M. Bisova To: Senior Polymeric Containment Engineer F. G. Thothenberg  Dear Fritz Germanovich, We appear to have switched places. Date: Day 214, Year 2 From: NOT SPECIFIED To: NOT SENT  Hi, my love. I don't know when you'll read this, or if you'll read it at all. It's like a year has passed since I wrote my note. Maybe they told you I died, but that's not true. My grandmother told me there's a proven method of transferring thoughts where you write down even the things you're afraid to say, then roll it up and stick it in a bottle to send out into the world. Maybe that's all gibberish and fantasy, but there's certain strength in getting these words down. A life spent expecting to die soon seemed unbearable to me. The truth can mend your life, but the truth can break your heart too. I acted like a total fool, but since I've volunteered for these experiments, I understand how wrong I was. Please forgive me for leaving the ones I love most for so long. Don't beat yourself up about the past. I hope you can forgive me. I just wanted to be a good person, and I probably need one last chance. Now I don't even recognize myself. I wish everything could be the way it was before, but I'll never be the same again. It's as if they've made me into someone else, and not just on the outside. I'll try to come back as soon as they patch me up, but everyone says I can't leave. This is a secret facility. I've already studied the security here, but it's no simple task. I'd like to promise that everything will be okay, but I can't. Only hope can keep me together.

Date: March 25, 1955 From: Stabilization Lab Manager O. Garipova To: #ANKH_staff  Dear colleagues, Technician F. Polnek has been transferred to a secure institution out of necessity. Date: November 25, 1954 From: Head Power Plant Engineer Y. Shevchik To: #engineering_department  Dear colleagues, Tired of answering the many questions from every new group of employees like, "Why are there military weapons underground?" When an energy surplus arises, that energy needs to be put somewhere. Given that a high-powered laser is a voracious energy consumer, we have an arrangement that allows us to use excess energy during periods when the main devices are not operating at full power. Otherwise, we would suffer unnecessary power losses and would need astronomical funds to supply energy for the devices and the laser. 2. It is not just a scientific device. The laser defends the complex from orbital dangers, asteroids, and hostile rocket launches. It can change the trajectory of a celestial body or neutralize a target. 3. Consequently, it is a strategic object. Stealth and defense from orbital strikes are more important than external access. Also, the rocks act as a kind of natural bunker.  Everything you see here is an infrastructural optimization, not an accident. P.S. Yes, I have memos in case other "genius" questions arise.  Y. Shevchik

Date: February 25, 1955 From: Junior Polymeric Containment Engineer A. I. Kovalyov To: L. N. Belova  My dear Lyusya, They picked me! Yes, for "that super-secret project"! I'll tell you, the rumors that were going around aren't anything close to the truth. I don't even know where we are—underground, under the water, or in the air like Chelomey? Sometimes, it feels like we're in Egypt. I'm joking, of course, but one of the developers (maybe even THE developer!) clearly loves this aesthetic. We even have sarcophagi here! Don't worry—they're just delivery containers. The scale is impressive. They've got the biggest polymeric mixer I've ever seen! There's also a supercomputer the size of a five-story house! Can you believe that?! Today was the phasotron test launch. An enclosed five-kilometer ring! The walls were shaking all over the building! Lyusya, I'm happy the way only a scientist can be.  I'll give you more details next time. Love you. Your Alik

Date: February 25, 1955 From: Crystal Complex Security Manager S. A. Poluyarov To: Junior Polymeric Containment Engineer A. I. Kovalyov  Alik, are you out of your goddamn mind? What "details"? Date: June 3, 1955 From: Behavioral Science Department Head N. Maklisov To: #Crystal_new_ones  Dear comrades, After reviewing the analysis and development prospects for the Crystal project, the committee has created the Cultural and Ethical Codex for the Polymeric Human. Date: March 3, 1955 From: Transformation Department Head Prof. A. Bisova To: #Duat_lab  Dear colleagues, I wanted to report on play patterns recorded over a two-week observation period. Days 1–7: introduction of movement games (tag, hide-and-seek, blind man's bluff). Results: rejected. Reason: lack of physical exhaustion and heightened sensations (hearing, smell, position in space) negate interest. Days 8–12: introduction of tabletop games (chess, Go, Battleship). Results: partially accepted but quickly abandoned. Reason: subjects calculate all possible moves in 0.1–0.3 seconds and don't get the desired mental workout. Days 12–14: subjects developed their own game. The rules were unclear, except that every participant could sacrifice their winnings so the whole group could maximize virtual resources while minimizing individual losses. When we tried introducing material rewards, their interest disappeared. Conclusions: The polymorphs are not interested in games with risk, punishment, or restriction mechanisms. Their game was not a form of relaxation or competition but rather a way to exchange internal idea structures. Recommendation: reassess the paradigm of "game as entertainment" in relation to the polymorphs.  Sincerely, Prof. A. M. Bisova

Date: January 3, 1955 From: Senior Caretaker of the Crystal Complex N. Tericheva To: Senior Fine-Tune Technician M. Kolesnikov  The central hub for activating neuropolymeric circuit exchange (CHANCE) is a next-gen stationary terminal designed to reconfigure and synchronize the neuropolymeric circuits of biomechanical organisms—first and foremost, polymorphs. These abilities can be activated and exchanged not only in polymorphs but also in human staff with at least B-level access. The process is based on molecular wave signal transmission, similar to the Argentum unit's combat glove. It's less powerful but has the added ability to directly interact with the polymorphs' polymer structure. While the system was originally designed for polymorphs, practical testing has shown that human operators can safely use the CHANCE to replace their own active modules. After successful trials, the Crystal's private scientific advisory council has approved the CHANCE installation in its buildings.

Date: May 31, 1955 From: Fine-Tuner D. Kobylkin To: Senior Fine-Tune Technician M. Kolesnikov  Dear Comrade Manager, the complaints about the conveyor belt are understandable, but I'm not the right person to talk to. The conveyor belt lives its own damn life. Can you at least give them safety harnesses or something? Or, preferably, a new brain. Basically, I've taken some measures and have managed to restore some order, but I would appreciate it if you chewed their asses out on your end.

Date: Day 34, Year 3 From: NOT SPECIFIED To: NOT SENT  After observations by myself and my new comrades, I can say that mortal man has finally triumphed over death and become a god created by the hands of humanity itself. The polymeric body is the vessel for a new soul. It's the rebirth of man into something like a god and hero of antiquity, except it's real and not mythological.
