The goddess Aphrodite was the epitome of beauty, but every crystal being has a beauty within that reflects our new, wonderful world. Now, when we look at the stars, we know the gods are not there. We are them, and more. The new architect of the Universe is a polymeric human, with a godly fire in their heart. The old gods are dead. We are the new gods, made of polymer, neurons, and will.

Date: October 4, 1954 From: Transformation Department Head Prof. A. M. Bisova To: Facility 3826 Chief Directorate Inspector D. S. Tkachenko  Dear Comrade Inspector, I'll get right to the point: yes, at first, animals were imported as subjects for testing polymeric connections and modeling a human-free ecosystem. Have you ever seen a wolf lick a sheep like it was her cub? The polymer has made them feel like they're all one equal society. We have inadvertently obtained living proof that intellect does not belong exclusively to man. And now you're suggesting that we "dispose of" these animals? The staff is firmly against such an order, no matter who gave this vile command. You can complain, you can threaten, but trust me, I'll find a way to answer. And then you'll only have yourself to blame.  Prof. A. M. Bisova

Date: June 5, 1955 From: Vavilov Complex Assistant Manager V. Zolotukhin To: Captain 1st Rank A. Grigoriev  I'm glad you understood the task and found a quick solution. Date: June 5, 1955 From: Duat Lab Psy-Architect V. Vasilevsky To: Duat Lab Psy-Architect A. Pak  Morning, Alexey. You're probably at breakfast right now, so let me entertain you a little. Date: Day 61, Year 3 From: Transformation Department Head Prof. A. M. Bisova To: Senior Duat Lab Psy-Architect I. A. Sahkhat; CC: Senior Polymeric Containment Engineer F. G. Date: Day 66, Year 3 From: Senior Caretaker of the Crystal Complex N. Tericheva To: Head of Crystal Complex Medjay Service N. Davydov  Hello, dear comrade! Date: April 7, 1954 From: Lab Assistant S. Pozharnov To: Acting Sakhalin Testing Ground Security Manager I. Paramonov  Dear Ilya Grigorievich, please don't think that I'm snitching again, but I had to inform you about the extremely odd behavior being exhibited by Comrade P. Date: June 7, 1955 From: Head of Crystal Complex Medjay Service N. Davydov To: Crystal Complex Security Manager S. A. Poluyarov  Dear Captain, I had it with Thothenberg! Date: Day 71, Year 3 From: Senior Writer M. Kolyvanov To: Transformation Department Head Prof. A. M. Bisova  Dear high priestess, So far, you haven't presented a single idea regarding what to name these "crystal" people. Not only are they wandering around like ghosts, but we also have no idea how to refer to them in our clerical documents! Date: March 8, 1955 From: Senior Duat Lab Psy-Architect I. Sahkhat To: Transformation Department Head Prof. A. M. Bisova; CC: Senior Polymeric Containment Engineer F. G. Thothenberg  Dear Anna Mikhailovna, I didn't want to worry unnecessarily, but it's already been ten days since our department became involved in the experiments. We're observing strange things here. Series No. 04 prototypes have become apathetic. Their communication with service staff has dropped to the absolute minimum. One of the subjects (No. 04A-D) spent days motionless, unresponsive to stimuli, but vital signs were normal. The other prototypes are no better. Their oxytocin and dopamine levels are practically nonexistent in response to social interaction. The sexual receptors lack any arousal from visual stimuli. The same goes for direct stimulation. My biggest concern is that this is not a defect but rather systemic. Perhaps the transparency of their bodies brings with it a loss of the symbolic "I." There is no shell, which means no border between "myself" and "others." I'm worried. Oh, and happy International Women's Day!  I. A. Sahkhat

Date: February 8, 1955 From: Senior Polymeric Ka-ntainment Engineer F. G. Thothenberg To: Transformation Department Head Prof. A. M. Bisova  Dear Anna Mikhailovna, my enlightened priestess, I am not disappointed in the least. This is exactly what I needed. Just look at the scale and depth: "While antiquated at first glance, they are in the ancient Egyptian death cult, where all current life is but a precursor to real life: the afterlife. ... What is the mortal body if not a shell for the mind? A restrictive, ramshackle, delicate shell. And what is living in a human society if not the daily preparation for a better life? Right now, we are closer than ever to that better life. Is it the afterlife? That depends on which side you're looking from." Can you believe that? This explains absolutely everything! EVERYTHING!  F. G. Thoth-enberg

Date: June 9, 1955 From: Ship's Doctor D. Suleimanov To: Captain 1st Rank A. Grigoriev  Dear Captain, after a cursory observation of the ship's officer, I suspect something is wrong with him. It's likely piblokto. The symptoms fit.  The social alienation is obvious. He walks around mumbling and steers clear of everyone. Then he becomes agitated and starts rhythmically tapping on surfaces with his fingers. The trouble is, we're too south for an Arctic-based hysteria. Also, I've never seen anyone go through every stage of it in just a few hours. In any case, I will conduct a full examination and keep you informed. P.S. Something about his tapping struck me as familiar. It was Morse Code. There's one thing he taps regularly without hesitation: "I'm still alive." As an experiment, I tapped back, "So am I." Without even looking at me, he responded, "Run away!" Captain, I wanted to.

Date: Day 90, Year 3 From: P. Rybakov To: Senior Caretaker of the Crystal Complex N. Tericheva  Dear Nadezhda Artemyevna, Forgive me for the bluntness. You're a sensible person, which is why I'm writing. Wasn't Crystal created for those whom no one else could help? People like me who have given their bodies to serve the Motherland. Comrades who lost parts of themselves in the war, in the mines, in industrial furnaces. For us, this isn't immortality but a chance to return to society. Now there's talk that this technology will be given first and foremost to the "valuable" ones. I am sorry, but is a simple machinist who saved the workshop from a fire not as valuable? Is the old woman who raised three scientists in wartime less important than an administrative paper pusher? Why are we becoming devalued? When did our losses stop having meaning? I sincerely hope these are all just stupid rumors. But if this complex is now serving only "valuable people," then as soon as I get out of quarantine I'll be writing to Pravda, Moskovskij Komsomolets, and television. This is not humane. This is not Soviet.  Pyotr Grigorievich Rybakov, veteran

Date: Day 167, Year 3 From: Osiris Vessel Keeper Thoth To: #Crystal_mausoleum  Glass hands creep across the dial and a swarm of Pharaoh's flies can be seen through my transparent insides. I'm a man of action, and your attempts to stop progress will turn to ashes of deserts! The development of the Bygones has ground to a halt. The path the gods walk is now open to the New Ones! We do not fear the future. We are the future. Everything happened for a reason, and now I actually see Duat. Every evening, when the light goes out in the lab, the hallways fill with sand. It pours down from the ventilation grilles, rustles through bearing grease, scrapes across the blades of nano-scalpels. The grains gather into silhouettes, and the first is Anubis. His body is blacker than obsidian, but his eyes burn like coals in a hot furnace. He leans toward me, and I hear the thunder of ancient pistons. This is the beating of my own heart weighed on Maat's golden scales. A scarab crawls within me, rolling a glowing ball of my reborn ego. Formulas are recorded on my transparent palms. I remember applying them, just like a cartouche tattoo. I wanted to understand and explain, but now there is no point in that. My body is clearer than water. My heart is lighter than a feather.  Osiris Vessel Keeper, Thoth

A hard-working specialist from the younger generation of doctors, Eduard Furman does everything in his power to try to attain his mentor Dr. Domov's level of skill. Patients and colleagues have often noticed Furman subconsciously copying not only his superior's work style, but also his ordinary mannerisms, gestures, and even speech. Comrade Furman does not yet fully realize that he has already earned a place at the hospital by dint of his hard work and has no need to imitate Comrade Domov.

Dr. Lizova is an outstanding specialist in the field of endocrinology. She could have become an excellent practitioner, but she preferred management to medicine and is now the Pavlov Complex Hospital's head physician. Thanks to her leadership skills, she has managed to not only assemble a team of top-notch specialists, but also attract the attention of Comrade Pavlov himself. The hospital is now one of the most high-tech stationary medical facilities overseen personally by Pavlov.

Addendum to lecture material, based on Moscow State University student questions:  ...Regarding the mannerisms of our production models, it's all much simpler and, as usual, a bit more absurd.  Rafiks and mittens The hands of the Rafik model were modified from cryogenic facility robots, in which the algorithm "cold = danger" reduced the risk of harm from supercooling. In the firmware of the model RAF-6, the algorithm concluded the opposite association: "safety = warmth." Later, in civilian modifications, the behavioral matrix was not eliminated. As such, mittens became something of a fashion signature for Rafiks.  Vovas and mustaches The mustaches were a side effect of earlier experiments on visual identification. The engineers decided to add mustaches because users trusted the Vovas that had them. The self-training algorithms solidified the component as an important social indicator among Vovas.  Tereshkovas and their "cute" tendencies Initially, Tereshkovas were given an "emotional mirror" behavioral template that included a positive reaction to round shapes, soft tones, and a conflict-free behavioral model. As a result of a too-flexible empathy matrix, this template developed into real attraction, which could be called love.  However, it is important to understand that none of this is "humanity," but an echo of old firmware left over from when we taught machines to imitate humans to make people more comfortable with them. Though I must admit, you will occasionally see a Vova trimming its mustache in front of a mirror. I wonder, have we inadvertently created something more than a simple machine?  Prof. Lebedev

Shy polymorph: Uh, hello. I'm sorry to contact you like this with a recording, but... well, it's easier for me.  Shy polymorph: So, I'm new here. I was just recently placed in this body and... I have a request.  Shy polymorph: Okay, here goes. Could you, you know, build a restroom for us polymorphs? I know we don't need them, and our chemical processes are different, but...  Shy polymorph: I don't need it physiologically speaking, but for... for psychological purposes, I guess.  Shy polymorph: I mean, we are practically see-through, and you're observing us constantly. Restrooms... are a place to be alone. A place for privacy. Being alone with your thoughts.  Shy polymorph: A chair in the corner of a windowless room would be fine. I know you have a few rooms still unassigned. Maybe one of those?  Shy polymorph: Just... please don't tell anyone about it, okay?

Cream pie: Hello, my dear lovers of fresh and sweet cream pies! Today, we'll be cooking up a dish that'll make your oven steam up way faster than a glass of cool wine in warm hands.  Cream pie: Let's start by massaging the dough. I knead it through my fingers, making sure to caress every inch.  Cream pie: Now, grip a thick, hard sausage! Arrange pieces of it into rings around the dough's base.  Cream pie: Mmm, tomatoes. Ripe, firm, and so juicy. Oh, just imagine me playing with these tomatoes! Oh, they feel so nice and taut! Slice them and put them on top of the sausage.  Cream pie: Now I'm gently touching the head of cheese. I'm squeezing it as good and as hard as I can!  Cream pie: Next, drip olive oil over everything! Nice and glistening. Now... stuff it... ooooh... in the oven...  Cream pie: Now we can relax and wait for the pizza to be ready. Don't rush it. Sometimes, the anticipation is as delicious as the main course.

A celebrated engineer and machine builder, Makhnyov did not leave Facility 3826 when he retired, but continued working there, becoming the well-known and well-liked cable car station master at Vavilov Complex. His pleasant, amiable demeanor always puts smiles on the faces of employees as they hurry to work.  "Without Ludwig, this place would grind to a halt!" is a common phrase among passengers.

An engineer, roboticist, and programmer, Petrov began his career at the roboticized Maya Plisetskaya Theater as it was in the midst of its most transformative upgrades. He has shown himself to be a talented and inventive specialist with a certain amount of creative vision. Comrade Petrov has an excellent grasp of art, which has helped him make friends with the director of the roboticized theater, as well as Facility 3826 Deputy Director Michael Stockhausen, a well-known aesthete and patron of the arts. Thanks to his friendship with Comrade Stockhausen, Petrov was able to demonstrate his skills and the fruits of his academic labor to Comrade Sechenov himself. The head of the Facility greatly appreciated the young programmer's hard work and pragmatism, which led to Petrov being assigned to a leading position in his scientific team dedicated to the development of the Kollektiv 2.0 neural network.  He has since been found guilty of treason and sentenced to community service at Vavilov Complex.  #.KEY: //Msg. start// Screw you and your military swagger, Major! You'll never take me alive! I'm a superior being. You're just a jackal!//Msg. end//#REG.ENTRY: #June111955

Unfortunately, not all new employees are able to successfully integrate with the Facility 3826 team—especially if their position fails to meet their own expectations. The keeper of the legendary Aniva, a Japanese lighthouse from the distant eastern island of Sakhalin, Khozin has found himself unable to adapt to modern reality. Nostalgia for his old life, robot patrols, and the occasional tour groups from Almaty, Kazakhstan that pass his lighthouse have rendered this lonely, unsociable man even more introverted.

Like the entire interactive entertainment and middleware development department, this high-profile specialist of Polish and Greek descent has made every effort to help the Facility achieve its goals. Overcoming all the challenges of his intense and important work easily and with a smile, Comrade Altupolis proudly delivered a truly fascinating video game that has since become part of Kollektiv 2.0's software. As a result, he received accolades from his coworkers, took a vacation to Gagra, Georgia, and received a financial incentive from the Facility. Huzzah, Comrades! Glory to the heroes of Soviet labor, and long live video games!

Comrade Grabov's career began in 1941, when he was forced to drive a train carrying coal to the front lines while under Fascist fire despite having no experience. His uncle had taken him inside the engineer's cabin, but was heavily wounded by shrapnel from an exploding shell. Instead of panicking, the young nephew took the controls and managed to drive the train to the troops' position. This feat earned him a medal for bravery and set the young man on his life's path, which would always be bound up with trains. Grabov is fond of saying that "a train needs to ride the track to the end, to the last inch, and get the job done."

A typical engineering manager, Veritayev is strict, rude, loud, and demanding, but still quite competent and knowledgeable. The VDNH's technical staff is all under his direction, and his team has won several awards for superior performance despite the odd magnet-related mishap.

Working with Nechaev is better than not working at all. Curiously, most of my calculations end with him being one of the key variables resulting in a bright future. Our enemy is intelligent, clever, and cunning. He can—and will—strike in the most vulnerable spots. It's why I used an atypical, absurd, and crude neurobeacon to capture the test subject's primal reactions and experiences. I surmise it's far easier to remember seeing a raving madman on the street than, say, a meek accountant. The experiment is simple: activate a spontaneous stimulation leading to behavioral feedback, which creates a subjective experience in the subconscious. Agent P-3's reaction was recorded: first irritation, then an attempt at rationalization, followed by persistent nervous anger, and, finally, stabilization. Agent P-3's handlers have trained him to have high trust in the "logic of the system." This gives us a chance to channel his aggression in the right direction. P.S. As for the trickster's shape, it's rather simple. Sasha Privalov's insight inspired me: "One should not stoop to his level. The goose is not on level ground with the swine."  Prof. Lebedev

A junior Vavilov employee, Neyelova was recruited to Facility 3826 as a lab assistant due to her excellent performance in graduate school and various internships. She is interested in genetic modification, has studied botany, and has proven to be very responsible and driven. Her husband is currently serving as a Navy watchman in Kamchatka.

Raguzin is a young Vavilov engineer and an orphan who lost his parents to the Brown Plague during the war. He is an introvert, but also a very talented genetic engineer who has set the record as the youngest specialist at the Facility and the one who has performed the most successful genetic experiments. His most interesting papers, which include "Mobile Plant-Based Cattle Feed" and "Self-Replicating, Fast-Growing Plants," have won him a number of awards.

Nikolai Vavilov is a geneticist and botanist. He led botanical expeditions to Western Europe, Asia, Africa, North America, and South America that have enabled him to identify the original sites of the morphogenesis of plants. Vavilov laid the foundation for the study of plant immunity and discovered the law of the homological series in the hereditary variation of organisms. He oversaw the creation of the world's largest collection of cultivated plant seeds, created the system used by the Soviet government to test varieties of cultivated plants, and formulated the principles that now govern the activities of the country's primary agrarian sciences center.  Now in charge of Vavilov Complex, one of the largest complexes of Facility 3826, Vavilov breeds new species of plants in order to expand our planet's agricultural potential and prepare for the ongoing plan to colonize outer space.

An appointee from Leningrad, Smirnov was tasked by the Party with monitoring individual Complex employees. Despite the fact that his role as a "snitch" is well known, he is respected by his coworkers, first and foremost as a host of leisure activities and educational clubs.

A legendary scholar of imperial Russia and later the Soviet Union, Pavlov is the oldest employee of Facility 3826, having reached the truly remarkable age of 106. He met Sechenov soon before his last heart operation, which saved the inventor's life. He is in charge of the complex that bears his name, where he studies the capabilities of biological species, programmable mutations, and progressive medicine.

I'm writing this so I don't go insane from the stillness. Everything is silent: the radio, the THOUGHT device, the engine, the infected soldiers trapped on the lower deck. Even my own mind is beginning to go quiet. But goddamn it, WHY IS THE ARMY SILENT? Aren't they just civilian robots? Any soldier who's had their footwraps and machine gun for more than a day could tear those robots to pieces. Sure, there are a lot of them. They're everywhere. But so are we! The biggest army in the world, and silence! Either something happened at the highest level, or I have one other terrible thought.  What if they're just sitting there in Moscow, waiting until we die here? Given Sechenov and the politicians' squabbles, it wouldn't surprise me if they could help us and just don't want to.
Behavioral Psychology of Polymerized Subjects Department Manager
Radio of the Future Department Manager

Soviet radio performer Vera Vershinina's incredible, poignant voice became legendary throughout the Soviet Union when she was chosen to become the voice of the Deimos OS virtual assistant in June 1950. Comrade Vershinina's personality and vocal tone was so well-liked at the Chelomey Design Bureau that she quickly become the official voice of Facility 3826. If you talk to a computer, it will answer you in Comrade Vershinina's voice.

Burak was recently appointed to the post of exhibit curator by the Ministry of Culture. Despite his magnificent recommendations and excellent work history, he has struggled to fit in at the strict, buttoned-down VDNH. The HR department receives complaints about his rudeness, excessive familiarity, and condescending attitude toward employees on a nearly weekly basis. However, upper management has been extremely positive about the new hire, noting his fresh perspective on how exhibit pieces are presented and implemented. "Comrade Burak has such an innovative view of things that impetuous new behaviors are always just a step away," said a complaint against Comrade Burak filed on behalf of the VDNH Tour Guide Union.

A German scientist of Jewish descent, Stockhausen worked as a doctor in Berlin during the war. He lived through the first outbreaks of the Brown Plague and was later saved by Soviet soldiers. Prior to his infection, he had an incredible memory—a fact his coworkers could attest to—but lost this ability after the onset of the illness and never demonstrated it again (although he does not regret the loss).  Thanks to his scientific and organizational talents, Stockhausen's career enjoyed a startlingly rapid ascent. He was recruited to the Facility in order to fill a quota for scientists from the German Soviet Socialist Republic and quickly earned Sechenov's respect. Despite his German pedantry and a certain degree of snobbishness, he remains one of the best-known—and best-liked—members of the Facility 3826 team. He is perfectly capable of speaking Russian without an accent, but chooses to "sound German" in order to remind people of his origins.

Sherman was sent to Vavilov in order to fill a quota for specialists from the German Soviet Socialist Republic. Her primary specialization isn't plants or genes, but rather designing essential equipment and reviewing requests from specialists in various fields.

Few people have met the director of the AoC, who is also a leading Soviet programmer and the creator of the Aldan supercomputer. Most employees don't even know that this man exists, but he has actually replaced Comrade Lebedev as the head of the Academy of Consequences' top-secret Neptune facility.

Although his last name is derived from the Russian word for "caramel," Karamelkin is anything but sweet. Everyone knows that he is excessively rude to rule-breakers and can even get physical with more serious violators. Despite this, there is no denying that the theft of drugs and equipment has been reduced fourfold since he assumed his current position. Comrade Karamelkin is fully cognizant of his place at the Facility and in the world at large. Some aspects of his personality suggest a high degree of discipline, while others are nothing more than bad habits. "Everything's fine," Karamelkin mutters before returning to his usual duties.

It stands to reason that logical intelligence must be followed by emotional intelligence. And yet, most cybernetic scientists fail to take this step when they build their interaction models with artificial intelligence. If we are to create a powerful mind to work with humans, shouldn't it have features that humans can relate to? And so I have cracked it. Built on the power and the analytical strength of the quantum Aldan machine, NORA also contains a human personality. After the tragedy in Bulgaria, I have come to possess a mold of sorts, an emotional map, you could say. Normally, it is something a human develops through complex interactions over decades. Now, I have one, complete with preferences and desires.  It is better than a mechanical consciousness—a living mind created not just from the mathematics of algorithms, but from a tapestry of feelings. Was my obtaining of this mold ethical? I cannot say. Whatever rules I have violated will stay my personal secret. What remains is a practical solution. That is without dispute.  Prof. Lebedev

Comrade Lastochkin is not a traditional theater director. Better known as "Stefan," Lastochkin has had a stunning career, starting out as an office manager and becoming the head of what is perhaps the most famous theater in the world. In less than a year, unique performances such as "The Binding Screws of Friendship," "In the Vice of Passion," and the modern classic "Electric Origins" have become sensations among fans of avant-garde art. However, his narcissism, shady dealings, and despotic management style have set many theater employees at odds with the ambitious new director.

The theater's new office manager, Surkov is an elderly, experienced man who has worked at the Bolshoi and overseen performances on the front lines for soldiers. An honest, but also one-dimensional and somewhat cantankerous old man, Surkov often has harsh words for management and anyone else who draws his ire.

A recent hire, Vishnevskaya was brought on to replace a senior programmer who was fired for inappropriate conduct. She is known as a suffragette, social activist, and active proponent of women's rights. Vishnevskaya is beloved by her coworkers for her responsibility and friendliness.

REQUIRED READING FOR ALL NEW ARRIVALS!  Dear comrades, welcome to the future! The years spent developing Facility 3826 have brought us all to this ceremonious moment. Soon you will enter a new world, one where you will forget the hardships and deprivations of the past.  However, you may experience some dismay and doubts. What about your loved ones? What was your legacy? What does the future hold? Cast aside those unhelpful thoughts. Today, you are not losing your past. You are taking a bold step toward a horizon of prospects and unbelievable achievements!

Elena Krayeva is an exemplary Soviet citizen. Carefree and outgoing, she has long been a regular sight at Pavlov Complex cultural events. Along with her pleasant, friendly personality, Comrade Krayeva is also known for her great passion for her work and has been recognized as a hero of communist labor three years in a row.

One of the leading dog trainers in the Soviet Union, or "Pavlov's Dog," as he jokingly calls himself, Gromyko is a crucial member of the Facility 3826 staff. His published works on raising, training, and cross-breeding species have been translated into 64 languages, five of them by himself. However, despite all his talents and service to the Motherland, this modest dog breeder prefers the company of his four-legged friends to scientific debates. Especially valuable in light of Polymer-based biotechnology is his work on breeding and training martian and lunar "dogs," i.e. the Polymer-based organisms known as Plyusch, which, thanks to Comrade Gromyko's hard work and care, are now exemplary, obedient representatives of man's future interplanetary best friend.

One of the highest-ranking leaders in the Communist Party, Molotov is also the President of the Council of Ministers and a political opponent of Comrade Sechenov. A talented politician used to operate on an international scale, he was made the overseer of Facility 3826 by the CPSU Central Committee and the Council of Ministers.

One of the Facility's managers, Yelizarova is in charge of the VDNH's exhibits and visitor interaction. She stood out from the very beginning of her tenure at the Facility and is responsible for the creation of the VDNH. Rumor has it she had to personally convince Dr. Sechenov of the need for a museum, and her efforts have clearly been vindicated.

An experienced specialist in her department, Meglina has become quite well-known in certain circles thanks to her analytical mind. The valedictorian at her university, she has a gift for studying available materials and drawing exceedingly refined, elegant conclusions from them. Just give Yevgenia Meglina a few data points, and she'll spit out an analysis before you can blink.

An experienced specialist, Nazarov is one of the creators of Polymer-based express printing technology, which has increased the speed of the Facility's printing dozens of times over. He runs the VDNH's printing department, but is actually responsible for all printed material throughout the Facility.

Yefremov admits that he dreamed of becoming an actor as a child, but, after working in security, he has dedicated his life to the theater in another capacity. His magnificent record as a Facility 3826 roboticist began with repairing robotic ballerinas at the Plisetskaya Theater, but he was soon promoted to a more senior position at the VDNH. His coworkers consider him an extremely friendly, fun-loving, and inventive expert with a natural sense of flair.

It may sound macabre, but for morgue supervisor Gireyev, dead people are the love of his life. Having begun his career as a gravedigger at a Moscow cemetery in imperial Russia before the revolution, Gireyev's career has involved exhuming bodies, destroying the corpses of people killed by the Brown Plague, and overseeing funerals for unknown soldiers after the war. He rarely makes jokes, but is "more comfortable with the dead, since no one's ever had his life ruined by a corpse."

Although he has no interest whatsoever in the theater, Papkin knows robots and complex technological processes like the back of his hand. An agronomist and food service engineer, Zolotukhin was one of the first to speak out against Lysenko and his theory before Vavilov's theories had been approved. A businesslike man of few words, he has demonstrated a high level of professionalism when it comes to overseeing the activities of the complex.

Dr. Sechenov is a neurosurgeon, roboticist, inventor, and philanthropist. He began his career studying collective intelligence at the Soviet Academy of Medical Sciences' Brain Research Center, where he hoped to engineer a perfect way of life for the communal cities of the future. He worked on the ManKind Project before the war, but dedicated himself to studying the Polymer after it was discovered. After World War II he was put in charge of a robotics program designed to make up for the country's significant lack of human resources and took over Facility 3826 on Comrade Stalin's personal order. Once Soviet robots had been distributed throughout the world, Comrade Sechenov become the Minister of Industry. His revolutionary discovery of the Polymer's capacity for mimetic adaption made it possible to inject this extraordinarily promising new technology into human tissues. This laid the framework for what would later become Kollektiv 2.0, a merging of humans and machines into a single neural network capable of fundamentally transforming and improving the everyday lives of not just Soviet citizens, but the entire world.

Zakharov was Sechenov's best friend and colleague (although many have remarked that the scientists were bound more by a strong professional relationship than anything else, and no one ever saw any evidence of real friendship between them). He worked with him on most of his innovations, starting before the war and ending with the discovery of the Neuropolymer. Unlike Sechenov, Zakharov was introverted and antisocial. Journalists and colleagues have emphasized that while Sechenov was driven by a desire to help mankind, Zakharov only seemed to derive pleasure from learning the laws of the universe and subjugating them to his intellect. Unfortunately, his misanthropy and indifference to his own well-being led him to ignore safety protocols, and he was killed during one of his own experiments.

During their year and a half at the Academy, these twin brothers have become its unspoken symbol. Despite their lackadaisical attitude, excessive frivolity, and constant jibes at their coworkers' expense, the Klimovs are skilled specialists who have made a number of improvements to the statistics-gathering process that vastly increased its efficiency. However, they told no one about this for the first two months, preferring to spend their newfound free time on video games designed to look like work software.

A former regional war commissar in the Kazakh Soviet Socialist Republic, Mukhtarev was assigned to Vavilov Complex following his early retirement due to an accident. According to his fellow servicemen and subordinates, not even the robots and architects know every inch of the complex as well as he does.

As the village overseer, Abdurakhimov routinely plans leisure and practical activities for employees lodged in Forester Village. He is extremely responsible and scrupulous, but has been prosecuted for embezzlement in the past. Because of this, he is extremely quick to curtail any attempt to use resources for anything other than their officially designated purpose.

Formerly prima ballerina Ryzhova's best friend, now a soloist at the Maya Plisetskaya Theater, Tamara Artemenkova had had to fill in for her ex-friend in lead roles when the latter was unable to make it to a performance (primarily due to capriciousness and a refusal to share the stage with robots, of course). Despite the enormous competition between human and robot ballerinas, Artemenkova loves and respects her mechanical colleagues and proudly boasts about sharing the stage with them, seeing it as an unprecedented artistic experiment.

Valeria Ryzhova has dreamed of being a ballerina for as long as she can remember. When she was nine, she could already perform flawless battements and cabriolet, albeit at the cost of a broken chandelier or two. After graduating from the Moscow Ballet Academy with honors, she was recruited to the Maya Plisetskaya Theater, where she very quickly became the most sought-after dancer. However, following the appearance of robot dancers, her popularity gradually began to wane. Deeply conflicted, she eventually came out against performances that included both human and robot ballerinas. No one took her position particularly seriously, since Ryzhova was known for being difficult, and the theater's staff had already grown accustomed to her flights of fancy. "You've cried wolf too many times!" Artistic Director Stefan Lastochkin once told his protégée.

A WWII veteran who lost his leg in the war and experienced extreme PTSD as a result. He has a very negative attitude toward robots, colleagues who sympathize with his disability, and prisoners sentenced to community service. He is unsociable and rude, but regularly receives recognition for his tireless dedication to duty, which he uses to prove over and over again to himself and others that he is still fit for work.

Ismailov is a war veteran and retired officer. He is a gruff, straightforward, and crude man with an excellent reputation as a security expert. His obvious character flaws include a tendency to promote his friends, especially those who served with him in the military, which often leads to conflict with the VDNH's other managers.

Despite his parents' and teachers' expectations, Petelka did not become a famous physicist. Although he certainly had the potential, the young man's exceptional mind and fantastic imagination ultimately allowed his reach to exceed his grasp. Comrade Petelka learned about robots from a newspaper article even before the war and never stopped fantasizing about them. Petelka did end up becoming a physicist, although he was never famous. He worked with Comrade Filimonenko on a cold Polymer synthesis project, was an excellent robot configuration technician at the Maya Plisetskaya Theater, and even made his way to the secret departments of the AoC, where he truly felt his "insignificance before the vastness of the cosmos."  "I understand this world perfectly. We're all just grains of sand in an ocean of electrical connections," Comrade Petelka declared before retiring from science, effective immediately. But he did not leave the Facility. Having returned to his duties configuring robots and servicing the theater's electrical grid, Petelka is, perhaps more than any other Soviet citizen, eagerly anticipating the Kollektiv 2,0 update that will utterly efface the boundary between human cognition and the capabilities of robots.  "We're all just electric currents, just ones and zeroes" is a favorite phrase of Petelka's, who often spends his free time in the theater's coat check room observing his favorite robot, the coat check girl.

A top-notch neurosurgeon and colleague of Zakharov's, Dr. Filatova is a talented Academy employee and a specialist known for her intelligence and subtly manipulative behavior. After her mentor's death, she continued to work on integrating human consciousness into the Kollektiv 2.0 network. Her social rating has been reduced due to her romantic relationship with Viktor Petrov.

The required algorithm has already been configured in the robots. There will be no second warning! This decision has been approved by management and is not subject to appeal.

Date: June 15, 1955 From: Triton Complex Security Manager A. Kasperovich To: Triton Complex Security Manager A. Kasperovich  To be honest, all the events of the last days are a blur. All these deaths, yelling, screaming as if through dense water... Every day, I thank fate, chance, or someone's will that we've managed to survive here at Triton. But to speak frankly, I'm grateful most of all that the MOR-4Y are autonomous and haven't turned against us... When one of the devices disappeared from the dock, I had already abandoned all hope. The soldiers were discussing which would be more difficult to handle: the Rafiks, Belyashes, or Dewdrops... Praise science that none of them—and us!—has had to see what the MORs are capable of if they were to go crazy like the rest of the machines. Damn it. I'm getting scared even as I write this. It's swimming around somewhere out there, after all. And who knows what could pop into that "orca brain"...

Date: June 15, 1955 From: AoC Radio of the Future Department Manager A.V. Lebedev To: Facility 3826 General Director D. Sechenov  I don't know if there's anyone on the other side of the screen, Dmitry, but I hope you'll receive my message. Fight fire with fire, as they say. As such, I am currently studying NORA's primary recombination protocols. I'm mulling over how to cluster reboot her system and, possibly, get the perfect weapon for this monstrous massacre... With a bit of luck, my creation will allow us to solve the problem created by yours. Although I don't believe in luck, I do believe in statistics. And despite all the consternation, it's on our side.
Date: May 17, 1955 From: Department of Ornithology Assistant Professor M. Illarionova To: Sakhalin Testing Ground Security Manager I. Paramonov

Date: May 17, 1955 From: Triton Complex Director J. Vernaya To: #for_publication  The multipurpose autonomous mechanism MOR-4Y is designed for underwater operation. It is practically the Burav's younger sibling but has a set of distinguishing characteristics. The majority of them are driven by the experimental conditions under which the mechanism must operate. In particular, the MOR-4Y is characterized by its highly durable body capable of withstanding an incredible amount of water pressure. Its astonishing mobility, provided by its independent, maneuverable modules, allows it to be used in such complex and precise work as laying underwater cables and pipes. Furthermore, if necessary, the MOR-4Y is fully capable of working on dry land, albeit with somewhat less efficiency. However, the main difference—and main achievement of Soviet scientific genius—lies in the construction of the MOR-4Y using a live orca brain. This is what makes such a complex system work.

Date: May 17, 1955 From: Senior Mechanic P. Plekhanov To: #techstaff_Triton  Hi, guys. Last weekend, the bottom of this place collapsed, revealing quite a large cavern. We have temporarily covered it with a grille so no one accidentally falls in since the situation there is hazardous. If you really need to enter (and when I say "really," I mean REALLY), the locking mechanism on the grille is connected to the control panel. The button is labeled. But again, it would be best to go around it. P.S. There is another entrance to the cave in one of the observation stations. But you are also prohibited from using that! I will send another notification once everything is repaired.

Date: June 18, 1955 From: Unknown Sender To: Technician N. Kholmetsky  The password is "Buyan," you, paranoiacs, be damned. Basically, buddy, you don't know me, and I don't know you, but the informed people said you're not just the best—you're the only one who can do this. This narcissistic crate must be ready to use as soon as it gets to Triton. And it should be able to make both a paper airplane and a combat fighter, understand?

Date: June 2, 1955 From: Assistant on Cultural and Educational Activities I. Kharlamov To: #facility_employees  Colleagues, this is a reminder that we will be holding a jubilee in September for the 10th anniversary of the Facility's Komsomol organization creation. The Komsomol cell from the Vavilov Complex will help us deal with all the arrangements—I am confident in this aspect. However, everyone else is expected to come up with suggestions for our organization's anthem. We've been around for 10 years, but don't have our own anthem, which I consider a failure. A Komsomol organization without an anthem is like children without names. I am putting particular faith in our Atomic Python stand-up club comedians. As a former comedian myself, I know you are creative, so you're the ones who have to answer first and foremost. I suggest you don't drag your feet. Summer is going by quickly.

Date: June 2, 1955 From: Triton Complex Director J. Vernaya To: Triton Complex Archives Curator D. Saydov  This morning, I read an article from a foreign newspaper about how Soviet science is changing the world and stumbled upon a curious fact: did you know that there is a Church of Kollektiv movement? Seriously, that's what it's called. It popped up three days after the launch. They support universal polymerization, hold virtual church services through the THOUGHT device, and do other things of that nature. On the one hand, it's commendable, since people are promoting the ideas of Kollektiv and such. On the other, a church?! Are you kidding me? You know, we're fighting against religion extolling mankind and its intellect and opening new horizons of science! And now someone's promoting that to the rank of "cult" and building a new religion around the ideas of progress and humanism. A couple of years ago, the USA also (loosely) combined religious and scientific ideas and got themselves the Church of Scientology. Quite an odious enterprise. To be honest, I don't think we need to follow that precedent.

Date: June 2, 1955 From: Senior Mechanic P. Plekhanov To: #techstaff_Triton  Hi, guys and gals (yes, ladies, I got it)! Updated instructions for the particularly forgetful (I'm talking about you, Grigorovich and Sevastyanova). There is an autonomous supply vessel floating on the lake. Are the lights broken or the cable gone? Use the control panel to send a signal. Need a new tool? Use the control panel to send a signal. Forgot your lunch on the shore? Well, you get it. The system will drop everything you need in a container. Other than organizational skills. You'll have to use your own!

Date: May 22, 1955 From: Senior Mechanic P. Plekhanov To: #techstaff_Triton  Hey, guys, I want to remind you of three simple things that, to be frank, I am tired of reminding you. First: the regular inspections of power sources like Candles at station number 13 were not put in place for no reason. Make sure they are always available there. Second: these freaking trilobites pick up everything that has even a speck of polymer, so keep the entrances to the observation stations closed. And third, if a trilobite still manages to get its pincers on a Candle, do not put yourself in harm's way. Call a specialist. Otherwise, we'll have to get the daredevil out of the trash again!

Date: April 23, 1955 From: Planning Engineer N. Zamuruev To: Triton Complex Director J. Vernaya  Dear Julia Albertovna, my colleagues and I have been discussing the construction of an underwater, swimming city similar to the flying cities. And we are so enthralled with this idea that we're ready to move from idle discussions to formalizing ideas and blueprints. Just imagine: Nereus, a giant underwater swimming complex for researchers and engineers. Like the Icarus Platform for Chelomey, but underwater. Extraction of oil and resources, exploring the sea floor, collecting biomaterials, and maybe even discovering new species! A project that aims to find new potential for humanity at the bottom of the sea will once again underscore the triumph of scientific thought.

Date: May 23, 1955 From: Head of the Inspectorate at the Ministry of Industry of the USSR A. Yakovlev To: Chelomey Complex Secretary D. Tyomin  Comrade Tyomin! We have discussed this already! I do not even accompany my children on the roller coaster or the Ferris wheel at the amusement park, and you yet continue to plot against me. How long must I tolerate this abuse? Every time you send the Turbine for me, I get soaked with sweat! There isn't even a parachute in your flying Wunderwaffe. I won't ask whose idea it was to fly ordinary cars in the sky, but I beg of you, my dear fellow: could you please arrange a less terrifying means of transport for me? Even a helicopter! As long as there is a parachute on board.

Date: March 25, 1955 From: Senior Lab Tech M. Isayeva To: Experimental Analysis of Behavior Group Director S. Mirina  Of all the individuals from group 58B, the most trainable is M236, Notus. He figured out the control panels within three days, completes tasks precisely, and ignores neural reagents as positive reinforcement, preferring to communicate. I believe he has learned to understand body language after observing me for a month. He really loves fish cakes... just like Nikolai, my love... It happened by chance. He stole one from me while I was having a quick lunch by the pool, and now he asks for them constantly.  P.S. Stepanida, I'm begging you not to put Notus through tests with punishment. I implore you not to hurt him. Please!

Date: May 25, 1955 From: Junior Lab Assistant V. Aleynikova To: #vetdepartment_Triton  Dear colleagues, please be advised: do not read the dolphins Russian classics, and do not allow them to watch scary movies! The mentality of dolphins is much more flexible and nuanced than ours. They easily pick up on negative emotions and become anxious and depressed. Please try to avoid philosophical subjects and deep discourse. It is best to only communicate with them simply, briefly, using jokes and funny remarks.

Date: May 25, 1955 From Triton Complex Director J. Vernaya To: Bioengineering Department Manager Dr. A. Morov  Dear Andrey Sergeyevich, I'm also not too pleased that your bioengineering achievement has been called trilobites. But that's how it goes, as you know. If it stuck, not even acid could erase it. Now, some criticism. Yes, the hybrids have successfully completed the tests and proven themselves capable of collecting garbage from the lake floor. They reliably find polymeric and neuropolymeric waste and deliver it for processing. But! They naturally drag in everything that contains polymer! They tried to carry off a polymerized employee, technician Korotkov, when he dove to the bottom while swimming in the lake. Please look into this.  P.S. In the official documentation, your project is registered as Limparius. It means "cleaner" in Latin, in case you weren't aware!

Date: May 27, 1955 From: Senior Oceanographer A. Polikarpova To: Triton Complex Director J. Vernaya  Put an end to the sarcasm and inappropriate irony! Yes, I am in all seriousness suggesting we use polymer whales as logical centers for the OCO project. So what? Picture this: enormous, majestic animals sailing through near-earth orbit. Their polymeric bodies harmonize with their unbelievably powerful brains, which we've improved with our neurotechnology. Isn't that impressive? You're saying, "Compared to the compact satellites and spacecraft, the idea to fill orbit with whales seems absurd and labor-consuming." When have we ever been afraid of work? Tell that to Comrade Stockhausen, who personally caught the first gray whale for Sechenov and laid the foundation for our work! The cosmic ocean, teeming with satellite whales, would be an incredibly powerful cultural phenomenon that's hard to imagine. It would be a sincere triumph of scientific genius and aesthetics. After all, it was the aesthetic part that made all the products and developments of Facility 3826 so recognizable!

Date: February 28, 1955 From: Salacia Complex Animation Studio, L. Atamanovsky To: Assistant Manager of the Triton Complex Medical Block A. Ragin  I can't take this anymore, Andrey. I'm tired. This Stockhausen guy is criticizing our work again! The director was even fired. Now we're wrapping up two new animated pieces with Artesha on orders from your complex. He says there's "not enough motivational propaganda for work and labor and too much artistic license." I suggested making something new, like an animated piece based on famous fairy tales, which he also vetoed. There's no life with his censorship. I'm going to ask for an exchange of experiences abroad, in the Land of the Rising Sun. I saw a few works from there—the animation is spectacular. And how are you doing at your challenging post?  P.S. Remember how I asked for a couple of tickets to the premiere of the new Lukomorye dolphin show? Were you able to get them?

Date: May 29, 1955 From: Trade Union Chairman E. Daukantas To: Manager of Testing Ground's Subsidiary Farming Y. Dynin #CC: Sakhalin Testing Ground Security Manager I. Paramonov  Yevgeny! There's a collective proposal to make our coastal area a leisure spot for Facility employees. You see, another bunch of vacationers from Mendeleev came back and are now in low spirits. They say there's real service there! They say there's recreation! We don't need much to start. A boat station with a pier, chaise longues, a couple of catamarans, and grills. Cover the shore with fine-grain sand or pebbles. It won't be cheap, of course (I've asked the accounting department to draft an appraisal), but the morale of the team is more valuable than temporary money. As the former manager of a Pioneers' camp, you know this better than I do. I'm planning to raise the issue on Monday at the staff meeting, so keep that in mind.  Hello and hugs to your Galina. Marina and I are expecting you for a barbecue on Saturday. Georgadze promised to treat us to marinated mutton!

Date: May 29, 1955 From: Senior Oceanographer A. Polikarpova To: Triton Complex Director J. Vernaya  Please be advised that ecologists have discovered a new mutation in a sea creature that has clearly arisen from neuropolymer supersaturation in water masses. This species (Octopus vulgaris, or octopus) can usually live out of the water for almost a day, but the subspecies discovered can go without for over a week. Additionally, this new "mutant" displays extremely aggressive behavior. In an attempt to obtain new neuropolymer compounds, it has been observed damaging cables, sneaking into the complex, and even stalking divers. Its self-preservation and breeding instincts are superseded by its hunger for neuropolymer. The females even use their own egg clutches to attack fish, dolphins, and divers with their offspring (we've named them octopups). I strongly insist that the issue of the swift extermination of the entire population be raised at the next meeting.

Date: June 3, 1955 From: Junior Lab Assistant V. Aleynikova To: Lab Tech R. Ivanova  Hi, Rimma! Yes, I know we just saw each other. I wanted to share an idea with you. Remember how we used to celebrate Neptune Day at Artek? It dawned on me today—why don't we bring that tradition here to Triton? Or even better, to the whole Neptune Complex! Imagine me and you as mermaids, the men in the costumes of sea devils, and Comrade Dynin in a sailor's shirt with a seaweed beard! I think it'd be symbolic and really fun. These celebrations really bring the team together. What do you think? Is it worth talking to Daukantas so he can bring the idea to the management? Or is it stupid?

Date: June 3, 1955 From: Land Oversight Services Manager D. Kirilenko To: Facility 3826 General Director D. Sechenov  Dear Dr. Sechenov, we have successfully concluded negotiations with representatives of the local administration of the Party secretariat. They have agreed to transfer a large portion of land adjacent to Facility 3826 for our purposes. However, we urgently need you to select the position for the new testing ground. Based on the objectives, we will claim the southern, western, or northern part of the surrounding area. P.S. Regarding naming suggestions for the testing ground: "Technology," "Science," "Progress," or "Foundry." P.P.S. Comrade Shalchinov, People's Deputy of Ozyorsk city, has requested a designated videodrome area on one of our testing grounds. He said you'd understand.

Date: June 3, 1955 From: Sakhalin Complex Senior Ranger P. Livadny To: Sakhalin Testing Ground Security Manager I. Paramonov  Dear Ilya Grigorievich, the pranksters are getting out of hand again. It's been two weeks since your lads caught the vandal who mutilated the beautiful Malus sieversii with the inappropriate and vulgar inscription "Yulia + Kolya." Well, we've got a new trouble! Someone excessively joyful has gotten into the habit of affixing eyes to the trees. Trust me, it looks quite creepy, especially at night! Not to mention that it causes damage to valuable and sometimes rare plants. Yesterday, a group of mycology students went out to the campsite at dusk and they were scared half to death. This is downright disgraceful, I'd say! Somewhere, the hills have eyes, as they say, so now our trees do? You must find out the identity of this prankster and let me know. I will prepare a report for their place of work or study. Then we'll see who's laughing.

Date: May 30, 1955 From: Triton Complex Head Veterinarian A. Sergeyeva To: Proposal Implementation Department Manager I. Kulibin  Dear Ivan Viktorovich, I have a quick question. Our dolphin Nale raves about soccer. He dreams of having legs. Sometimes, he gets so lost in his daydreams that he skips meals. As a result, he's become gloomy and is losing weight. I was thinking... Can your department invent some kind of... let's say, inverted dive suite with mechanical legs? Not to win any awards, other than the award of our daydreamer's good mood. I'm afraid he might get really sad.

Date: May 30, 1955 From: Triton Complex Director J. Vernaya To: #engineering_department  Comrade engineers, in relation to the launch of Kollektiv 2.0, the time has come to begin the fourth phase of our space program. Our goal is Venus. The structure of our underwater base will become the technology for residential complexes on the planet. Over the last year, we have significantly updated our knowledge base regarding the atmosphere on Venus. We have taken into account aspects like radiation, gas flow, and hydroponic systems. I am giving the order to immediately ask all remaining complexes to provide all the help they can in developing protection from externalities. P.S. Remember how we were arguing with the guys from Vavilov what Sechenov would colonize faster: Mars or Venus? Let's show those botanists how the space race is won!

Date: June 4, 1955 From: AoC Radio of the Future Department Manager A.V. Lebedev To: Facility 3826 General Director D. Sechenov  Dmitry, the most important question in history is not "why," "how," or "who." The most important question is "when." And this "when" is formed from the assembly of all questions, like a puzzle. Catch my drift? If not, then time will show, as they say. P.S. As a source of inspiration, here's my take on Sir Newton's apple.

Date: June 5, 1955 From: Facility 3826 General Director D. Sechenov To: AoC Radio of the Future Department Manager A.V. Lebedev  Alexey, you were absolutely right comparing it to a puzzle. The image of a Rubik's Cube wouldn't leave my mind until it dawned on me. The future must be approached holistically. The whole is greater than the sum of its parts, after all, and prognostic problems should be solved through complex analysis. So yes, you have my approval to prepare research studies, and I will personally supervise them.

Date: June 5, 1955 From: Triton Complex Security Manager A. Kasperovich To: #biomodeling_department  Comrades, I looked over the documentation regarding the test run of your "armored crabs." I am denying this request. I understand that you want to add them to deep-water operations before New Year's, but as they are still exhibiting aggressive behavior and you are not able to fully control them, I cannot approve even a test run. We have a global event on our horizon and have no margin for even the smallest error. P.S. You already have tons of robots. What do you need oversized crabs for?
Date: June 5, 1955 From: Senior Lab Tech M. Isayeva To: N. Fadeyeva

Date: February 5, 1955 From: Regular Psychologist N. Fadeyeva To: Senior Oceanographer A. Polikarpova  At your request, I have conducted a psychological analysis on M. Isayeva regarding her readiness to return to work. Her depression and muteness related to the shock of her husband, N. Isayev, going missing at sea two years ago remains. I believe that returning to work will have a positive impact on M. Isayeva's health, and I recommend working with animals. In particular, there are studies on the therapeutic effect of dolphins on people with psychological trauma. As I understand, you have no shortage of dolphins.  P.S. I'd like to write an article on how depression affects the chemical reactions in the brain when communicating with animals. I will personally oversee this case.

Date: June 6, 1955 From: Assistant Manager of the Triton Complex Medical Block A. Ragin To: #observation_log  The lab assistant, Evgeny Khudobrovov, came in today. According to available information, he was in the cafeteria with his colleagues from the Advanced Research department, celebrating their comrade's dissertation defense. He had tea with cake and sweets. Was heavy on the sweets. He became queasy and excused himself to the bathroom. Then he disappeared. He was discovered two hours later in a hallway of the complex. Khudobrovov was trying to lick the walls and take a bite out of the doors. He insisted they were made of cookies. It's clear from analysis that Khudobrovov's body contains an excess of trans fats, lysergine, maltodextrin, sucralose, amylopectine, and a variety of other substances. Preliminary diagnosis: organic hallucinosis and paranoid schizophrenia. Polysaccharide toxicity (TBC) acted as the catalyst. An odd case. Will need to take samples to check. Consult with complex psychologist, B. Sobol.

Date: June 6, 1955 From: Chelomey Complex Assistant Secretary E. Nikishin To: Chelomey Complex Secretary D. Tyomin  Daniil, could you ever tell the difference in behavior between the Twins? Everyone says they're like two peas in a pod, reflections in a mirror, and other such "cut from the same cloth" expressions. But I've been working here for several years now, so I can spot the differences. Left is somewhat more... graceful, I guess. Her movements are smoother. More fluid. I think "more poetic" is the right wording, especially considering the more functional character and rigidity of Right. It's not glaring, of course, but if you look closely, the difference between these allegedly identical machines is huge. I wonder if Sechenov designed them that way...

Date: June 6, 1955 From: Triton Complex Security Manager A. Kasperovich To: #staff_Triton  On the night of June 5 to 6, for unknown reasons, there was an unscheduled opening of the block A gateway, which caused the dock to flood and damaged the robots. The reasons for this event are under investigation. According to preliminary data, a dolphin with the marking M236 has also gone missing. If anyone has any information regarding this event or the location of senior lab tech Marina Isayeva, please contact security services.

Date: June 6, 1955 From: Senior Ichthyologist and Whale Biologist I. Kotlyarov To: #shore_monitoring_services  One of our whales has disappeared. Let's skip all the jokes like, "how did you manage to lose a whale?!" Yes, we lost him. Something startled him, and the whale busted out of his enclosure and headed for the shore, which, as you are aware, is highly abnormal. Could you please launch Drofas or send someone to the shore to look for Semyon? Yes, the whale's name is Semyon! Thanks in advance. P.S. And no mocking! Or you won't get any caviar for the next month!

Date: April 7, 1955 From: Triton Complex Security Manager A. Kasperovich To: Experimental Analysis of Behavior Group Director S. Mirina  Dear Stepanida Vitalyevna, one of your employees has been visiting the dolphinarium at night on a regular basis using a universal pass. A young lady who has not been captured by the cameras, but whose heels can be heard clicking on the floor. I fully understand that science is above all else, but the safety standards for overnight work are set for a reason. Please confirm how much longer this will go on so we can adjust our work accordingly. Thank you.

Date: June 7, 1955 From: M. Karingina To: E. Rukavitsyna  Lena, I was right when I wrote about the acid rain! The only problem is that things have gotten much worse. Valya's husband, who works at Chelomey as the foreman of the repair team, told me privately that they're conducting an examination after the Icarus incident, and there's some kind of toxic substance leaking from either the braking or balancer system! You're drowning us from above, as they say, and with acidity too. So Ignat and I are going further from Chelomey for now. Probably to Sochi for a week. And yes, I covered my mother's dahlias so they won't die from this "water."

Date: June 7, 1955 From: Triton Complex Security Manager A. Kasperovich To: Senior Ichthyologist and Whale Biologist I. Kotlyarov  Comrade Kotlyarov, we have a problem with the dolphins here. Your employees have analyzed their behavior at my request and discovered that they are becoming jealous of the robots. Naturally, they try to damage and even break them. In particular, two dolphins named Tristan and Isolde. As we do not want to harm your animals, we are requesting that you take immediate action!

Date: June 7, 1955 From: Proposal Implementation Department Manager I. Kulibin To: Senior Mechanic of Proposal Implementation Department N. Lefty  Dear Nikolai Semyonovich, I hope you're well! Sergeyeva, our veterinarian, had an idea. It's technically flawed, but interesting. She asked if we could make an exoskeleton for Nale. He's the dolphin you were foaming at the mouth discussing soccer with. So, the dolphin's brain, apparently, is developed enough to use arms, except they don't need them. Do me a favor and draw up an exoskeleton with arms and thumbs based on the standard Belyash, would you? If we're lucky, we'll be able to integrate the dolphins into society to replace these hideous crabs I can't even stomach looking at. It's a nice, creative task. I submitted the order, so you can get to work. I'll have the documents with justification for the project after lunch.

Date: June 7, 1955 From: Triton Complex Director J. Vernaya To: #hr_department #hr_department_manager  I am writing to request that junior lab assistant Comrade Igor Valeryanovich Zhabov be immediately terminated or transferred to the Vavilov Complex for community service. You know why!

Date: March 7, 1955 From: Senior Lab Tech M. Isayeva To: #vetdepartment_Triton  A new batch of dolphins has arrived at the complex (5 total). A preliminary examination and vaccinations are required. F135, nickname Medea, female, light gray coloration, no distinguishing marks. F136, nickname Fly, female, light gray coloration, black spot on her nose. F137, nickname Snow White, female, albino. M235, nickname Zephyrus, male, silvery coloration, very active. M236, nickname Notus, male, dark gray coloration, communicative, familiar eyes.

Date: December 8, 1954 From: Senior Oceanographer A. Polikarpova To: Planning Engineer N. Zamuruev  Comrade Zamuruev, our discussions have brought me to an interesting conclusion. And since I'm on sick leave now, this idea is occupying my mind nearly all the time. We already know that the depths of the World Ocean are explored much less than the far side of the Moon. According to various data, only 2–5% of the World Ocean has been explored to this day. I am in no way dismissing Wizard's aspiration for the stars, but if we want to study a cold, endless abyss, then we need to look down, not up. Furthermore, the likelihood of finding intelligent life at the bottom of the sea is, by all estimations, far higher than in space. What if we, with our wars, industrial revolution, and polymer, are just noisy upstairs neighbors? It might be worth getting to know all the residents of our house before going to visit. P.S. I've also sent my thoughts to the AoC. Maybe they'll look into this question. Please reply. I really value your opinion!

Date: June 9, 1955 From: Assistant Manager of the Triton Complex Medical Block A. Ragin To: #observation_log  The body of a scuba diver, Grigory Kainov, was brought in today. The body had been at the bottom of the lake with a damaged scuba set for approximately 5–7 hours. Multiple lesions, cutting and tearing wounds. Right arm partially missing; it appears to have been eaten by fish or crabs. There was a lump in his stomach. When I opened it, some kind of octopuses jumped out (inexplicable). They began to run around the floor. I squished almost all of them. Scared the hell out of me. I need to urgently confirm with a specialist what these are and whether they have any kind of contagious capabilities. Preliminary diagnosis: too soon to tell. Contact Ganga complex's anatomic pathologist, W. Laurelova. She has also found something similar in a corpse this month (TBC). Note: I am incredibly tired. I want freedom. To sit on the deck drinking wine and discussing literature, and women in the evening.

Date: June XX, 19XX From: Special Projects Curator No. 315 To: Roboticist N. Kholmetsky  Autonomous collection and repair system DIY GUY-02 (abbr. for Do-It-Yourself Gear and Units Yielder). Technical data: classified Documentation: classified Integration logic: classified  There are three models in the DIY GUY series, each of which is a unique specimen of the engineering genius of Soviet scientists. Due to the enormous potential of these seemingly simple systems, all data about them is classified and is the responsibility of the roboticists assigned to the devices. The abbreviated name is not to be mentioned in documentation, so the robots have been given code names: Samodelkin, Lefty, and —DATA DELETED—. Currently, the Lefty system is being used on the combat testing grounds of New Earth, the Samodelkin system is in reserve at the Academy of Sciences in the capital, and —DATA DELETED— is located at —DATA DELETED—. Reminder to all engineers: to avoid information leaks, using the working name DIY GUY in any form of communication is prohibited.

Patients and colleagues have often noticed Furman subconsciously copying not only his superior's work style, but also his ordinary mannerisms, gestures, and even speech. Comrade Furman does not yet fully realize that he has already earned a place at the hospital by dint of his hard work and has no need to imitate Comrade Domov.

Zhabov, did you fall in or what?!  Zhabov: Yeah, yeah, I'm coming.
We'll get a handle on Muravyova!

A celebrated engineer and machine builder, Makhnyov did not leave Facility 3826 when he retired, but continued working there, becoming the well-known and well-liked cable car station master at Vavilov Complex. His pleasant, amiable demeanor always puts smiles on the faces of employees as they hurry to work.  "Without Ludwig, this place would grind to a halt!" is a common phrase among passengers.

An engineer, roboticist, and programmer, Petrov began his career at the roboticized Maya Plisetskaya Theater as it was in the midst of its most transformative upgrades. He has shown himself to be a talented and inventive specialist with a certain amount of creative vision. Comrade Petrov has an excellent grasp of art, which has helped him make friends with the director of the roboticized theater, as well as Facility 3826 Deputy Director Michael Stockhausen, a well-known aesthete and patron of the arts. Thanks to his friendship with Comrade Stockhausen, Petrov was able to demonstrate his skills and the fruits of his academic labor to Comrade Sechenov himself. The head of the Facility greatly appreciated the young programmer's hard work and pragmatism, which led to Petrov being assigned to a leading position in his scientific team dedicated to the development of the Kollektiv 2.0 neural network.  He has since been found guilty of treason and sentenced to community service at Vavilov Complex.  #.KEY: //Msg. start// Screw you and your military swagger, Major! You'll never take me alive! I'm a superior being. You're just a jackal!//Msg. end//#REG.ENTRY: #June111955

Unfortunately, not all new employees are able to successfully integrate with the Facility 3826 team—especially if their position fails to meet their own expectations. The keeper of the legendary Aniva, a Japanese lighthouse from the distant eastern island of Sakhalin, Khozin has found himself unable to adapt to modern reality. Nostalgia for his old life, robot patrols, and the occasional tour groups from Almaty, Kazakhstan that pass his lighthouse have rendered this lonely, unsociable man even more introverted.

Like the entire interactive entertainment and middleware development department, this high-profile specialist of Polish and Greek descent has made every effort to help the Facility achieve its goals. Overcoming all the challenges of his intense and important work easily and with a smile, Comrade Altupolis proudly delivered a truly fascinating video game that has since become part of Kollektiv 2.0's software. As a result, he received accolades from his coworkers, took a vacation to Gagra, Georgia, and received a financial incentive from the Facility. Huzzah, Comrades! Glory to the heroes of Soviet labor, and long live video games!

Comrade Grabov's career began in 1941, when he was forced to drive a train carrying coal to the front lines while under Fascist fire despite having no experience. His uncle had taken him inside the engineer's cabin, but was heavily wounded by shrapnel from an exploding shell. Instead of panicking, the young nephew took the controls and managed to drive the train to the troops' position. This feat earned him a medal for bravery and set the young man on his life's path, which would always be bound up with trains. Grabov is fond of saying that "a train needs to ride the track to the end, to the last inch, and get the job done."

A typical engineering manager, Veritayev is strict, rude, loud, and demanding, but still quite competent and knowledgeable. The VDNH's technical staff is all under his direction, and his team has won several awards for superior performance despite the odd magnet-related mishap.

A junior Vavilov employee, Neyelova was recruited to Facility 3826 as a lab assistant due to her excellent performance in graduate school and various internships. She is interested in genetic modification, has studied botany, and has proven to be very responsible and driven. Her husband is currently serving as a Navy watchman in Kamchatka.

Raguzin is a young Vavilov engineer and an orphan who lost his parents to the Brown Plague during the war. He is an introvert, but also a very talented genetic engineer who has set the record as the youngest specialist at the Facility and the one who has performed the most successful genetic experiments. His most interesting papers, which include "Mobile Plant-Based Cattle Feed" and "Self-Replicating, Fast-Growing Plants," have won him a number of awards.

Young technician: I'll record this for you, you're gonna die laughing. When he gets mad, he comes up with gems! Here.  Makar Kuzmich: Sweet mother of chaos, you blasted gizmo, open up already!  Young technician: Hey, Makar Kuzmich, what're you up in arms about now?  Makar Kuzmich: What kind of Moscow shit is this? There was a catastrophe here, corpses everywhere—hundreds of people died, if not thousands. But no! Drop everything and grab your butt to accept the urgent package from Moscow!  Young technician: Pff... Ahem... What package?  Makar Kuzmich: How the blunderfuck should I know? Some device as important as a fart in a windstorm... And there's a Mr. High-and-Mighty alongside it, hands cleaner than a showroom dummy!  Young technician: Maybe we need this device to help with the situation here?  Makar Kuzmich: I don't know, for fuck's sake!  Young technician: (snickers)... On whose orders?  Makar Kuzmich: I don't know a shit. But then, "Ensure the proper security of the Samodelkin device and access for the employee assigned." Badger shit!  Young technician: I told you, Kolya. When Kuzmich is angry, it's like a sudden improv show. He's like Jim Gaffigan, but swearing!
We lost a fucking whale! What bad luck!

Nikolai Vavilov is a geneticist and botanist. He led botanical expeditions to Western Europe, Asia, Africa, North America, and South America that have enabled him to identify the original sites of the morphogenesis of plants. Vavilov laid the foundation for the study of plant immunity and discovered the law of the homological series in the hereditary variation of organisms. He oversaw the creation of the world's largest collection of cultivated plant seeds, created the system used by the Soviet government to test varieties of cultivated plants, and formulated the principles that now govern the activities of the country's primary agrarian sciences center.  Now in charge of Vavilov Complex, one of the largest complexes of Facility 3826, Vavilov breeds new species of plants in order to expand our planet's agricultural potential and prepare for the ongoing plan to colonize outer space.

An appointee from Leningrad, Smirnov was tasked by the Party with monitoring individual Complex employees. Despite the fact that his role as a "snitch" is well known, he is respected by his coworkers, first and foremost as a host of leisure activities and educational clubs.

A legendary scholar of imperial Russia and later the Soviet Union, Pavlov is the oldest employee of Facility 3826, having reached the truly remarkable age of 106. He met Sechenov soon before his last heart operation, which saved the inventor's life. He is in charge of the complex that bears his name, where he studies the capabilities of biological species, programmable mutations, and progressive medicine.

Nastya: Dolphins are just like people! Each with their own personality, preferences, and idiosyncrasies.  Kolya: Huh.  Nastya: And the more they communicate with us, the more they can learn from us. Like Nale and his soccer...  Kolya: Yeah. Neat.  Nastya: And Lola? You haven't seen her, but... Nikolai? Nikola-a-ai?! Anyone home? Why are you looking at me like that?  Kolya: Your eyes are like supernovas, the way they shine. You're... on fire.  Hunter: Hey, kids, I... Oh... Sorry, didn't mean to interrupt.  Kolya: We were just talking about dolphins...  Nastya: Yeah, about dolphins.  Hunter: Right. I thought so.
